speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. It is said that a man is known by the company he keeps. I think the same is true of Governments. Canadians want desperately to think of themselves as winners. We need to, if we are to alter the public psychology which has been created by the economic policies of this Government. In view of this, a glance at the list of "winners" upon whom this Government has been bestowing our money is revealing-Chrysler, Dome, Maislin, Massey-Ferguson, and the list goes on. Indeed, the only contact that this Government has with the real winners in our corporate society is either to drive them out of the country or to sell them party memberships. Therefore, I wish to move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis):
That the Prime Minister and the Government reverse its thinking and attempt to reward success rather than failure as has been the case up to the present time.

speechtext:

That the Minister of Transport intervene in this matter in order to protect the interests of Legan Bus Lines and also the tourism industry in the Maritime Provinces.

subsubtopic: SCHOOL CONDITIONS ON ALBERTA RESERVE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, at the primary school on the Blackfoot Reserve near Gleichen, Alberta, children are crowded into classrooms in the school's basement, kitchen, and the principal's office. There are problems with lighting, heating and sanitation, and the fire marshal has expressed his concern. For years the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has known of the need for more classroom space. I therefore move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo):
That this House condemn the Government for its indifference to the educational needs of Indian children and instruct the Minister for Indian Affairs and Northern Development to ensure that portable classrooms are in operation by December 1 of this year, and to provide funds to start construction of new classrooms by next spring.

subsubtopic: LEVEL OF WAGES PAID TO CANADIAN WORKERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of pressing and honest public importance. The Citibank of New York recently released a study on international wage comparisons showing that Canadian workers have received lower wage increases over the last decade than nine of the ten countries surveyed, namely, Belgium, Britain, Denmark, France, West Germany, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, and Sweden, and further showing that Canadians have fallen from being the second highest to the second lowest paid amongst major industrial economies in that period. 1 therefore move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young):
That this House recognize that Canadian wage earners are not the cause of our current inflationary spiral.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this Liberal Government is moving in a heavy-handed way to penalize Canada's senior citizens by imposing on them a cutback in the indexing of their old age security. The Minister of National Health and Welfare, rather than taking up the fight on behalf of those pensioners, has bluntly told them that they must "lead the fight in the battle against inflation." That the Minister of National Health and Welfare demand of her colleagues that they lead the fight against inflation by reducing waste and unnecessary duplication in their respective Departments rather than unjustly laying this burden on the shoulders of Canada's elderly.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subsubtopic: CULTURAL AND SCIENTIFIC CONTACTS WITH SOVIET UNION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
My question, Madam Speaker, is for the Prime Minister. Canada has just had a high-level delegation at Moscow conducting negotiations that we are told are aimed at resuming cultural and scientific contacts that began under the Friendship Treaty of the Prime Minister with the U.S.S.R. in 1971. These exchanges were halted after the Afghanistan invasion in December 1979. We are told that the Government hopes to have a full range of exchanges with the Soviet Union before the end of 1983.
Has the Government made it a condition, as it should, that before Canada agrees to any improvement in its relations with the U.S.S.R., first the U.S.S.R. has to observe the Helsinki Accord, permit emigration to those who wish to emigrate, and treat properly people such as Mr. Shcharansky who are now suffering from inhumane imprisonment? Is it also a condition that the Soviet authorities withdraw their armed forces from Afghanistan and, finally, that they should encourage Poland to revoke martial law and release those who are now in prison for
COMMONS DEBATES_________________________ November 23, 1982
Oral Questions
supporting Solidarity? Are these conditions for any improvement in relations on our part?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: CULTURAL AND SCIENTIFIC CONTACTS WITH SOVIET UNION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am not aware of the detailed mandate given to the high-level committee that went to Moscow. 1 cannot say if all or some of these conditions are included in its negotiating mandate.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister is the head of the Government and some seem to think the fount of its wisdom, such as it is. Is the Prime Minister telling the House that he did not instruct or have his Secretary of State for External Affairs instruct this high-level delegation that the three conditions I mentioned, and I will not repeat them, are essential to be met by the U.S.S.R. before we can resume a warmer relationship with them? Did he not inform them of that.
Does he know that the Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs who headed the delegation is reported as having said in this morning's testimony that, "essentially there have been no visible signs of change in the Soviet attitudes in any of those three matters"? That being the case, will the Prime Minister inform the House whether we are going to proceed with this opening toward greater exchanges and the like, if there are no visible signs of any change in their position?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, if the Hon. Member is asking me whether I have seen the detailed mandate given to the delegation, the answer is I have not. As to the success or otherwise of the meeting that was held between officials in Moscow, I have no report on that.
I imagine I will receive one as soon as the delegation returns.

Madam Speaker, surely the delegation did not proceed to the U.S.S.R. without instructions from the Prime Minister's Government as to what they were to seek to achieve, and what Canadian conditions are before we can have an improved relationship with the U.S.S.R.? Surely the Prime Minister cannot expect us to accept that?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my supplementary question to the Prime Minister is this. According to the Deputy Minister we had no prior consultation with the United States or our NATO allies in this matter, nor did the Soviets initiate this rapprochement. In Munich, on his recent trip, the Prime Minister said that because of the death of Mr. Brezhnev it was a good chance, and I quote the Prime Minister, "to try and turn a new leaf with the Soviet Union". Why is the Prime Minister suggesting that we, and not the Soviet Union, should turn a new leaf? Is it the fault of the West that they invaded Afghanistan, that the Polish martial law tragedy has occurred, or that there are human
rights violations in Russia? Why should we be turning the new leaf and not the U.S.S.R.?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member misunderstood my previous answer. I did not say that the committee had no mandate. I said that I had not given it any specific mandate. I had not seen that mandate before it left. Obviously I discussed the matter with the Minister in general terms. The Secretary of State for External Affairs is at this moment chairing a ministerial meeting of the GATT in Geneva. I am sure he could answer these questions. I am telling the Hon. Member that I was not involved in the specifying of that particular mandate.
As to consultation with our allies, there probably has been some. I do not know. I do know that our allies do not consult us every time they want to make even the slightest gesture. I know there is a constant stream of American businessmen going to Moscow. There is a constant stream of Congressional and Senatorial delegations in Moscow, and they have not consulted me on that. I just want to make it clear that Canada should not be the only country that does not have any kind of relations with the Soviet Union. When something like 150 United States businessmen are in Moscow this week to do business, I do not think Canadians should forever renounce the possibility of having commercial transactions for the benefit of Canada in that country.

This was a high-level delegation of the Government of Canada, not of Canadian businessmen who are quite free to go to the U.S.S.R. just as are American businessmen. This was a Government delegation trying an apparent new initiative in the East-West over-all relationship.

BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-CANADA POST CORPORATION Mr. Bud Bradley (Haldimand-Norfolk) moved:
That this House, recognizing the importance of providing efficient, affordable, equitable mail service to all Canadians, and recognizing that Canada Post has reduced service while increasing its rates, condemns the Government for its failure to enforce the provisions of the Canada Post Corporation Act which require Canada Post to provide Canadians with adequate service at a reasonable cost.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I found it necessary to move such a motion and to speak to it because of the great concern felt by Hon. Members in my party and, I am sure, by those to our left for individual Canadians, Canadian charitable organizations, businesses and major corporations. Contrary to the beliefs of some Hon. Members opposite, we even have concern for the Canada Post Corporation. What is happening to the mail service in Canada is of great concern to those of us in the Progressive Conservative Party.
Let us look at the history of the Canada Post Corporation so that we will know where it came from. It was established in this House through the committee process to provide an adequate service at a reasonable cost. Its goal, to quote Mr. Warren and some of his executives, was to improve the postal service in this country. The Act which went through the House forming the Canada Post Corporation was agreed to by all parties of this House. All parties felt the need to remove this monster from the Department and the Government, and the need to form a new Crown corporation to handle the postal service in this country. We stand by our agreement today.
The definition of the term "letter" was not defined in the Act. It was also agreed by all parties in the House that that power would be given to the Canada Post Corporation to define what was mailable matter, what was not mailable matter, and what was a letter. The process agreed upon was that this definition would be arrived at by the Corporation. It would be placed in the Canada Gazette for an acceptable period and letters of representation from Canadians, organizations and businesses would be considered for a reasonable time so that amendments could be made and then referred to Governor in Council, and a final definition approved.
The rates for postal matters in Canada were also dealt with under the same format. It would be within the power of the Canada Post Corporation to determine what it felt was a reasonable rate in order to maintain the services of the post office in Canada. The procedure was the same. The rates would be gazetted, there would be a reasonable time in which to make representation and make amendments if necessary, and then a final decision would be reached by the Governor in Council.
That seems to be where the agreement between those of us on this side of the House and those on the opposite side ends. Certainly it is now a Crown corporation and it is being run as a
November 23, 1982

business. However, the Government of Canada must accept its responsibility as far as the post office and the country is concerned.
1 do not think I must remind too many Hon. Members opposite that the sum of $660 million of taxpayers' money is going to the Crown corporation this year to assist it in its operation. It is not attaining its goal to provide adequate service at reasonable cost.
What has happened to the Corporation this year, in which it has been a fledgling? First, the rates were increased some 76 per cent to 30 cents for first-class mail, which was totally unacceptable after such a devastating strike just prior to the increase, devastating not only to individuals and organizations but most certainly to small businesses in this country, sounding the death-knell for many of them.
The definition of "letter" was brought forth, and it was an unbelievable definition. Saturday rural mail has been stopped in all but Prince Edward Island, where the question is now being studied. Christmas card rates were brought up to the first-class rate of 30 cents, devastating to the card manufacturers and to people who send cards, but with a promise that the situation may change next year. If the promise that it may change next year is there, why not this year? Then there is our final rate increase, an additional 6 per cent, in line with the six and five program, to 32 cents. That represents an increase in the past year or so of some 82 per cent in postal rates. What private enterprise has been allowed to increase their rates some 82 per cent?
What is next for our Corporation? There is discussion of Saturday wicket closings in the post offices. There is talk about lay-offs of post office staff and there is discussion about reducing letter carrier routes and even the closure of some small post offices throughout the country.
What we have, Mr. Speaker, is less service at more cost. That is not acceptable to this Party. We have called for review of the Canada Post Corporation many times. We have called for it in the House of Commons, in the press and in letters. I have asked the Minister responsible for the Corporation about it in the House; I have asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and I have even asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister, trying to get someone to give an indication that this question would be referred to a Committee of the House to be discussed and considered, but to no avail.
I wrote a letter to the Prime Minister and perhaps I could read it into the record. I did not make it public and I did not release it to the Press. Because of the Prime Minister's concern and request for co-operation within the Parties, 1 felt that a letter directly to him with copies to the Minister and the President of the Corporation would be of some assistance and possibly get something done for us. I wrote as follows:
The Right Hon. Pierre-Elliott Trudeau, P.C., M.P.
Sir:
You may recall that on July 30th, 1982 I requested a study of the problems facing the Canada Post Corporation by a Committee of the House.
Mr. Warren has stated that the Corporation will be staying within the six and five per cent guidelines as far as an increase in rates is concerned. I feel this is a
Supply
very commendable and responsible stand. However, since only wage costs are controlled under the six and five per cent guidelines, major costs of vehicles, vehicle maintenance, fuel, building maintenance, etc. will undoubtedly exceed 6 per cent, resulting in costs which surpass income.
This situation will most certainly place considerable stress on Mr. Warren and his attempts to streamline the Corporation and improve efficiency. As well, he has the responsibility of reducing the post office deficit by some $260 million in a limited period of time. It would appear to me that when costs outstrip income, at a time when it is mandatory to decrease a huge deficit, there is no alternative but to reduce service. Reductions in service as initiated by the Corporation in recent weeks, and which will no doubt continue in the months to come, can only be accomplished at the expense of the customers.
Possibly we are asking too much to expect Mr. Warren to reduce his deficit so greatly during such difficult economic times. Perhaps consideration could be given to allowing an extension of the time table for the reduction of the deficit.
I am very concerned that in order to meet his deadline Mr. Warren will be forced to cause irreparable damage to the operation of the system, and also create hardships to customers and workers alike.
I would greatly appreciate it if serious consideration could be given to this matter.
I received a response and I would like to read that into the record:
Dr. T.A. Bradley, M.P.
Dear Dr. Bradley:
On behalf of the Prime Minister, I am writing to acknowledge receipt of your letter of September 13.
Please be assured that it will be brought to Mr. Trudeau's attention.
1 would have thought that a letter on a serious note to the Prime Minister of this country would have warranted a serious reply.
What has happened to this postal service and why has it happened? The deadline given to Mr. Warren when he took the job was that he was to reduce the deficit from some $660 million a year to zero within a time span of some four years, a totally impossible task. How many other Crown corporations are required to become self-sufficient in four years, or at all, of the some hundreds of Crown corporations owned by the Government of Canada? Could we consider the CNR or Air Canada or the CBC? If we look at each of those in turn, they are set up and established, as the post office was, to supply a service to all of the country, possibly subsidized if sufficient funds were not available. The CNR provides service to the north, to the east and to the west, with small branch lines throughout the Prairies, usually at a loss and usually subsidized. Air Canada provides service to the north, east and west and to the small strips, and quite often is subsidized. The CBC offers good programming and good listening to the areas of the north and all reaches of Canada, and it is certainly subsidized. Why not Canada Post?
It is the obligation of this Government to provide good postal service to Yukon, to Gravelbourg, Saskatchewan, to Corner Brook, Newfoundland. It is a responsibility and if it needs to be subsidized it should be subsidized. That is what Canada is about. That is what federalism is about. This is a great country, we should ensure that we work together with the Provinces in all areas to provide adequate service at reasonable cost.

November 23, 1982
Supply
If this $660 million reduction were to be removed from our national debt and it could be shown that it was removed from the debt, possibly the argument would not be so strong. Possibly Canadians could accept the extra cost, knowing that they are helping; but this is not going to happen. The Government would squander the money somewhere else, possibly buying licorice cigarettes for the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin).
What position has Mr. Warren been placed in in this fiscal year? He has a necessary reduction of some $260 million from his deficit; that amount must be trimmed this year. He has now been placed under six and five, in a very difficult economic time, where he has income of 6 per cent and most certainly expenses far in excess of the 6 per cent, possibly in the 12 per cent range.
What can he do, or, better than that, what must he do? What is he forced to do? He is forced to increase the rates, first to 30 cents, then to 32 cents. Why? Very obviously, to bring in money to reduce that deficit, to try to maintain the service that the Corporation has been providing. He has had to bring in a definition of a letter that is so tight, giving the Corporation such strict control over the volume of mail. Why? It was to bring in money and to improve the mail volume that has dropped off since the last mail strike and since the 30-cent stamp was brought in. He has had to reduce and in fact cut out Saturday rural delivery in order to cut the contracts of the rural carriers and save money. He has put Christmas cards at the first-class rate of 30 cents in order to glean an extra 10 or 15 cents a card to try to bail himself out of the pit. He is now looking at Saturday wicket closures, lay-offs, a reduction in letter carrier routes and the closure of small post offices in order to save wages, overtime and rental.
He is forced to do this in order to reach a goal that was set unrealistically by the Government in accordance with the Act passed by all parties in this House, but not with acceptance of that goal by all parties. It is being done with a reduction in service to the user of the post office. The rate increase was opposed by tens of thousands of individuals and businesses. That rate increase was soon after a postal strike which was devastating.
The definition of a letter is opposed by municipalities across this country such as Kitchener. Municipalities are being forced to deliver their municipal bills by Canada Post because of legislation by Order in Council.
Are we right? Are we as a Parliament right in telling the municipality which sends out municipal bills to municipal residents within the boundaries of that municipality for municipal goods provided by municipal staff that they must send those municipal bills to their municipal residents for municipal goods through Canada Post? We should take a long look at that because we are in the situation of forcing municipalities to increase their taxes to pay the extra cost for something they are being forced to do. The definition is being
protested by charitable and non-profit organizations. First they opposed the stamp and then the definition.
Today I received two letters which are an example of that opposition. One was from Capreol dated November 16. I suppose seven days for delivery of these is acceptable. I quote from the letter:
The proposed postal legislation, as described in The Citizen, November 6, 1982, page 21, will cause great financial hardship to the charitable organization to which I volunteer my time, La Leche League. We depend on being able to group various pieces of correspondence into one packet of first-class mail in order to carry on many aspects of our activities.
I feel sure that other non-profit organizations, such as La Leche League, will also be hurt, and that administrators in these organizations simply are not aware of the implications of the proposed legislation for them.
I have expressed my concern to the Hon. Andre Ouellet and to my own Member of Parliament. 1 appeal now to you, as the Post Office critic for the Progressive Conservative Party, to use any influence you can to make the situation known to the public who will be affected through the volunteer organizations which they support, and to have the legislation withdrawn because of its unfairness.
I was handed another letter by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie). 1 quote:
Dear Sir:
I am strongly opposed to the new Canada Post definition of a letter. I hope you can dissuade them from putting this definition into effect.
Rose Ryan.
Those are but two examples of hundreds of letters received from individuals, charitable organizations, businesses and companies throughout this country. There are over 300 businesses and corporations that oppose this definition. I wish to bring a couple to the attention of the House. In its letter to the Minister, The Canadian Bankers' Association said in part:
In our opinion, the task of properly defining the term "letter" and the scope of the Corporation's monopoly are of sufficient importance to justify careful consideration on the part of the Canadian public and corporate communities. We request that the Government consider the development of a special task force, or parliamentary committee to study the regulations, and the responses of interested parties, in order to satisfy the concerns that we feel and that we understand have been expressed by other interested persons concerning the effect that these regulations will have upon business and public interests in Canada.
I wish to quote from an article headed "Definition of letter held threat to small couriers":
General Motors Co. of Canada Ltd., Oshawa, Ont., uses private courier companies to move inter-office correspondence. The company has estimated that if the new definition becomes law, it would cost $3 million more a year to finance the system GM now has in place-
That $3 million is what it would cost General Motors to provide the same service being done internally. The couriers now carrying out this work would be unemployed. The money would not go to Canada Post because it does not have the facilities to provide the service required by General Motors. This would not only put men working in the courier system out
Thank you for any help you can give.
Yours truly,
Patricia Fraser.
Dear Sir:
Sincerely,
November 23, 1982

of work, but would be absorbed internally by General Motors. Canada Post would not receive any part of the $3 million.
These definitions were brought in in a package. Some amendments were then added. We now understand there are going to be more amendments, one to cover General Motors and one to cover security clearance. Still, an ad hoc committee has been formed to opppose this; these amendments are being opposed. Some of the members of the ad hoc committee which was formed on October 18 are as follows: the Consumers' Association of Canada, Canadian Federation of Independent Business, the Canadian Depository for Securities Limited, the Retail Council of Canada, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Canadian Bankers' Association, Conseil du Patronat du Quebec, the Motor Vehicle Manufacturers' Association, the Canadian Life and Health Insurance Association, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the financial Executives Institute of Canada, the Insurance Bureau of Canada, the Association of Canadian Financial Corporations, the Direct Sellers Association, the Toronto Stock Exchange and the Automobile Parts Manufacturers' Association. I quote in part from their brief. They-
-request that the Governor in Council refuse to approve the proposed "letter" regulation and submit it to the Privy Council, in order to allow a constructive dialogue among interested consumer and business organizations, the Post Corporation and the Government.
These are not small organizations. They oppose the definition. The definition of "letter" is like the Liberal budget brought down on June 28 by the Minister from Cape Breton Island. You throw as much into the boat as you can, shove it out in the water and check the waves. If the waves come over the gunwales, you throw some back. If more waves come over the gunwales, you throw more back. When the waves stop coming over the gunwales, you let it float. That is similar to what we have had happen with the definition of "letter".
We are told, Mr. Speaker, that this definition will not come into effect until April, 1983 so that business can adapt to the regulations that it sets out. If this is being put forward to April, 1983 so that business can adapt, obviously the Minister and the Corporation are aware of the problems this will bring to small business. That alone is sufficient reason to refer this definition to a special committee of this House so that we can hear from small business and these other organizations, and from individuals and charitable groups.
Taking away the facilities of Saturday rural delivery is opposed, Mr. Speaker. The Christmas card rate is opposed, not only by the card manufacturers of Canada and North America, but also by the individuals who send those cards to friends. Saturday wicket closing will be opposed. Rural people who work their farms come in to town on Saturdays to do their shopping and to pick up registered letters and parcels, notification of which they received during the week. There are the individuals who work in a large community and live in a small one, who are not in their community during the day and who need the Saturday wicket service to pick up their letters and parcels. People working in one part of a major centre such as
Supply
Toronto or Montreal but living in another part utilize Saturdays to pick up their registered letters and parcels.
Lay-offs will be opposed, as well as the reduction of letter carrier routes and the closure of some small post offices; and if one needs reinforcement of that, one could ask Mr. McGarry or Mr. Parrot as to the extent of the opposition to such a reduction of service. We on this side of the House are not saying that if we were still the Government we would not have given the same power and approved the same definition or thought the same rates to be necessary as this Government has, Mr. Speaker. But we feel that we would have had the foresight and the courage to say that possibly these things should be reconsidered and referred to a special committee of the House.
We applaud the task attempted by Mr. Warren, his Corporation and its workers. We applaud the honest effort, the realistic organization which has now been set up and the improved labour relations which have been initiated. We want to see that continued, Mr. Speaker, but it cannot under this Government's guidelines. It cannot carry on. We do not want to change Mr. Warren's direction. We just want it to be realistic.
This Government's policy towards the post office is off track and needs to be put back on the rails, headed in the proper direction. It is nice to be able to say it is a Crown Corporation now. It is independent of the Government. But that will not wash. It is not independent of the Government. The Government of Canada and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) are responsible for the Crown Corporation and for the taxpayers' money. They are responsible to make sure we have adequate postal service in this country at reasonable cost.
We are, therefore, calling on the Government to refuse the definition as proposed to it by the Canada Post Corporation and to refer the whole post office situation, after a year now of its operation, to a special committee of this House for review to see where we can go and what we can do to help it. We can then re-establish the parliamentary input by elected officials of this country to get the post office back on track. We could establish reasonable deficit reduction guidelines and Government response. We could maybe slide the deficit laterally for a year or two. We could maybe allow a longer period for it to be paid off. We could maybe authorize a permanent subsidy program, if necessary, we could also come up with a reasonable rate which is fair to business and to the Corporation. We could come up with a reasonable definition of "letter", after discussions with individuals, corporations, organizations, charitable groups and small businesses. We on this side of the House support the concept of the Canada Post Corporation, its management and its workers, but we want-no, we demand-an adequate level of service at reasonable cost to Canadians. This Government is preventing that from happening.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak to the proposal submitted by the postal critic of the Official Opposition. What struck me in the Hon. Member's speech is, that it is very easy for someone in the opposition to indulge in wishful thinking, without having to make difficult decisions. It is clear, Mr. Speaker, that the spokesman for the Progressive Conservative Party really has no solution to suggest, and that in fact, there are times when the Hon. Member is for the Canada Post Corporation and against the Government.
However, when the Corporation makes proposals under the Act that was passed here in Parliament and received the unanimous approval of this House, the Hon. Member no longer sides with the Corporation but with the businessmen and associations that have made representations to protest postal rate increases, just as he no longer sides with the Corporation but with those who objected to its definition of the term "letter". Clearly, the Hon. Member does not have the unanimous support of his own party, since what he is suggesting is that we increase the deficit and that Canadian taxpayers shoulder a greater share of the responsibility by taking on the deficit of the Canada Post Corporation. This is obviously not well received by his colleagues, the Members for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens), Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) and Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson), who are not in the House today, because if they were, they would object to what the Hon. Member has just told the House. And that is the beauty of being in the Opposition, the beauty of the Progressive Conservative Party, which is not in power and can afford to side with all parties at the same time, without having the responsibility for making important decisions.
Speaking of important decisions, I would like to announce that this morning, the Government of Canada made an important decision with regard to the definition of the term "letter". The House is aware, Mr. Speaker, that for several months the Government has been considering the draft definition of the term "letter" submitted by the Canada Post Corporation. To prepare this draft, the Corporation has been conducting consultations since last July with both individuals and a number of interested organizations. In the last few weeks, both the Corporation and the Government of Canada have received some excellent suggestions for amending the draft definition, especially in connection with bulk mail rates, handling of securities and the use of new technology in mail handling.
Since neither the Corporation nor the Governor in Council may amend the Act at this stage in order to incorporate the changes contemplated by the Corporation itself, and, of course, supported by the Government, it seems that now there is a preference for submitting a new draft definition that includes the desired amendments. That is what n,y colleague, the
Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Rompkey) told me in recent weeks on behalf of many associations and small businesses that wanted a more precise definition of the term "letter". I got the same message from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) who has received representations from many associations which were mentioned earlier by the Hon. Member. The same stand was taken by the Consumers Association, which made some interesting representations on amendments that would be desirable. So, since the Corporation is agreeable to amendments, and since the government is in favour, this morning Cabinet decided not to approve the wording of the draft regulation.
However, I wish to point out that the Government continues to support the concept of exclusive privilege for the Corporation, as well as the need to establish a precise definition of the term "letter" that will enable the Corporation to exercise that privilege. This is very important for the Corporation, because it must be able to provide a universal postal service throughout the country for all Canadians. This exclusive right is, in fact, the basis of all postal services throughout the world. It is not uniquely Canadian. The same exclusive right is shared by all postal administrations throughout the world. It is also one of the basic characteristics of public transit and public utilities. Thus, the Government is asking the Corporation to submit, as soon as possible, within the next few weeks, a revised draft regulation that could become effective on the same date as the first proposal was to take effect, that is, on April 1, 1983.
We hope that consultations will continue with major national associations, which have made known their views and submitted some excellent suggestions. As for the Hon. Member's proposal to refer the matter to a parliamentary committee, I may remind the Hon. Member that no such mechanism is provided under the Act. Besides, when we were discussing the issue during consideration of Bill C-42 to establish the Canada Post Corporation, I appeared before two parliamentary committees to talk about this. At one committee meeting,
I heard the position taken by one of the Hon. Member's colleagues, the Member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Beatty). At the other committee's meeting, I heard another of the Hon. In fact, after many discussions with both committees, it proved impossible to reconcile the views of all opposition Members, and especially those of the Progressive Conservative Members. I think that Parliament in its wisdom, by creating the Canada Post Corporation under Bill C-42, acknowledged that it was up to the Corporation to exercise its responsibilities, to take the initiative and to define what a letter should be. The

It would be appropriate in my view, at the beginning of this discussion, of the motion, to recall that Parliament attempted with Bill C-42 to create a social and economic base as much as a business entity when establishing the Canada Post Corporation. It must be remembered that the aim and duties assigned to the Corporation are complex, important and difficult. We should not underestimate the importance of this newly created corporation. Canada Post Corporation is the sixth largest employer in Canada, with some 60,000 employees, It operates 30 major establishments across the land and some 8,500 offices from sea to sea. Only one other Canadian company operates more trucks than Post Canada. The Corporation deals with no less that 20 unions and employee associations. Its turnover makes it the twentieth biggest business corporation in Canada. Therefore, Parliament established a highly important corporation when enacting Bill C-42 a few months ago.
It is much too soon in my view for the honourable member to take that corporation to task in this House. He is displaying a lack of tolerance and goodwill for the new corporation's directorship. Let us give them the time to prove themselves and then, if need be, we can criticize them. The Government, Mr. Speaker, has observed the Corporation to be following a consistent, deliberate course of action to improve its service levels since proclamation day in October, 1981. It has also made considerable progress in reducing its expenditures base.
1 would like to return to the remark I made in October, 1980 in this House, when I was speaking on second reading of Bill C-42. I said at the time that all the postal unions had been fully consulted in the development of Bill C-42. It was with very complete agreement that we proceeded with the transformation of the Post Office Department to Crown corporation status. 1 acknowledged in 1980 that we had managed through a decade of conflict in the Post Office Department, and that we were now hopefully entering a decade of harmony.
Things have not always been simple in the past year, but the management-labour relationships in the Corporation have improved substantially. The Corporation has consulted with the unions on every major policy decision. That consultation has been constructive and to good effect. 1 would remind the

Bill C-42 was developed with the extensive participation of Conservative Members as well. Allow me to quote a comment made in this House by the late Hon. Walter Dinsdale, a former Conservative critic of the post office. Bill C-42 does provide a good framework of enabling legislation. It does not, however, nor was it ever intended to, spell out, prescribe, or detail exactly how the Corporation would carry out its day-to-day business. It provided the framework for the Canada Post Corporation Board of Directors and management to establish the service base required to maintain good, dependable postal service in Canada.
We asked the Corporation to maintain basic postal service, while improving and extending its products and services. Canada Post is also supposed to consider the role of its employees in reaching its goals to ensure commitment and dedication to the job at hand and to ensure labour stability. All this is to be done while rates are kept competitive and while a three-quarters of a billion dollar deficit is eliminated.
In its mandate, the Corporation's new management team is faced with competing objectives which will require time, cooperation, understanding and good management.
This "bashing exercise" which is in vogue today is not useful. I regret very much that the Conservatives have chosen to use this Opposition day to blame the Corporation for bad service and for increased postal rates. It is too easy to blame the post office and to refuse to see the progress that has been made. It is easy to espouse the popular habit of downgrading the post office. I would have hoped for a more responsible attitude on the part of the Official Opposition.
With the establishment of Canada Post as a Crown Corporation, the new management team was able to mould its legislative mandate into the first real business plan that the post office has ever had. The top three priorities which emerged from this business plan are easily stated. They are: to improve service; to promote and maintain better human relations within the Corporation; and to work toward financial self-sufficiency.
How has the Corporation performed on the first priority, to improve service? I would be the first to suggest that the Corporation must improve its service. There is no doubt about

We are in the process of developing and improving a system designed to better organize mail handling operations in all our major post offices with a view to beefing up co-ordination between staff, equipment and type of mail.
The Official Opposition is talking about reduced services. How can they say that service has deteriorated? Just what evidence do they have to make such a statement? Let me turn now to a concrete example of improved service, Mr. Speaker. By the way, this improved service was made possible through the improving labour-management relationship that I spoke of earlier. Hon. On February 25, 1982 the Corporation announced that some 74,751 new homes and businesses would be served by some 170 additional letter carriers, beginning in April, 1982. These service improvements were made possible in large part by the increased postal rates which came into effect last January and by the introduction of productivity bargaining features in the 1982 contract reached with the Letter Carriers' Union of Canada. New letter carrier routes have been serviced in a number of cities across Canada.
It is worth taking a moment to recount the additional person-years which have been made available during a time of restraint. The union and management agreed to a number of productivity improvement measures, such as route restructuring and computerization of label redirection cards. The cost savings achieved from these and other productivity gains have provided some of the resources to meet service needs in other communities.
I take this major investment in improved delivery service as an early and concrete indication of the Corporation's commitment to its mandate and to its primary business objective, which is better postal service for all Canadians.
The Hon. Member briefly talked about Saturday rural delivery. He alluded to the question of the reduction of counter hours and espoused the idea that post offices will be closed. I do not know what he had in mind when he said this. Perhaps he was trying to scare people. One thing for sure is that the new Crown Corporation has a mandate to continue to give Canadians the type of services to which they have become accustomed. Not only will it continue this service but it will improve on it. This is what the Corporation is doing.
We will not involve ourselves in the day-to-day activities of the Corporation. I suppose the Hon. Member who saw his

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on today's motion which reads:
That this House, recognizing the importance of providing efficient, affordable, equitable mail service to all Canadians, and recognizing that Canada Post has reduced service while increasing its rates, condemns the Government for its failure to enforce the provisions of the Canada Post Corporation Act which require Canada Post to provide Canadians with adequate service at a reasonable cost.
This is a motion which I, and I believe the people of Canada, welcome.
1 would first like to say to the Minister, in particular, that my colleagues and I in this Party will be responsible. In being responsible, we will not attack the Canada Post Corporation nor the new management of that Corporation. Unlike the irresponsibility shown by Liberals and Conservatives in the House and across the country, irresponsibility which they have shown in numerable occasions, we will not attack the employees of the Corporation, whether they be inside workers or outside workers. We in the NDP want the Government, the Official Opposition and especially the Minister also to be responsible. In this respect I could not help but think that he sounded like the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) who, during a recent debate in the House, appeared so sensitive to attacks on his poor administration that he tried to pretend that Opposition Members, whether Tories or from the NDP, were attacking the employees of the Unemployment Insurance Commission instead of the policies of the Minister. Similarly, this Minister's policy towards the post office has left it with little alternative but to do the damage that is being done.
The result of the entire administration of Canada Post today has been some improvement to urban services, while there is a reduction in service, poorer service and I would suggest almost a sabotage of service in rural Canada. The effect the Government has had on the Canada Post Corporation as a result of the Minister's policies is typical of what happens when you give any city slicker lawyer the responsibility for essential services to rural Canada.
This is similar to the problem which was faced by VIA Rail after its services were separated. It was given an impossible mandate, starved of funds and resources and the passenger service was separated from the freight service which financially carried it. This same situation is happening to the post office, whereby the Government will likely eventually decide that the service to rural Canada has become uneconomic. It will build up a large public blacklash, especially from some of the private sector, which will then demand to be allowed to cream off those portions of the postal service which are
profitable and then leave the remaining Canadians, particularly those in the hinterland areas of Canada, with no service or with service at excessive cost which they cannot honestly be expected to bear.
I admit from the outset that there have been improvements in the Canada Post Corporation. One of these improvements has been an increase in mail delivered "on time" from approximately 80 per cent to 89 per cent during the last year. That is a significant improvement over a relatively short period. That is one of very few improvements. We have also seen many other basic services threatened.
I want to express my consternation and surprise at the Conservative Party for proposing a motion such as this. It takes a lot of nerve and even more hypocrisy for them to do this. The Conservatives have given their support to, and in fact called for many of the policies that the Government has agreed to follow-since the Government is acting like Tories so often-and that are causing the problems that exist within the Canadian postal service. 1 am amazed at the gall shown by those who proposed this motion when I consider what they have done previously.
Only a year ago we in the NDP, along with most Members from all Parties and certainly the vast majority of Canadians, were at least hopeful, if not optimistic, that the birth of the Canada Post Corporation, which had been demanded by so many for so long, could be a genuine rebirth of a once proud and efficient servant of the Canadian people. I say "hopefull" and not "optimistic" because we had some grave doubts due to what we believed to be the straitjacket of the unrealistic timetable of total and early self-imposed restraint and financial self-sufficiency which was demanded by the Government and supported by the Conservatives. The Government and those Members of the Official Opposition who sponsored the Government's policy were not satisfied with shackling this infant Corporation with the impossible demand of short-term self-sufficiency. They proceeded to starve it and batter it with the six and five program while hypocritically demanding that this infant Corporation rush to premature maturity and provide proper service to Canadians.
Let us examine what exactly was done. Michael Warren, President of Canada Post Corporation, has continually spelled out the three primary goals of the Corporation, as provided for under the Canada Post Corporation Act. The first goal is improved service; the second is improved human relations; the third is financial self-sufficiency. In the budget of November 12, 1981, a couple of budgets and one economic statement ago, the then Minister of Finance very clearly laid out the Government's expectations for financial self-sufficiency. From 198182, the Government expects the Canada Post Corporation to reduce its deficit of $620 million to zero by the year 1985-86. That is quite a demand at a time when the Government, the Official Opposition and this party are also apparently and hopefully committed to at least providing efficient and improved service across the country.

I and my Party urge them now to change course, to be flexible, to remove the impossible early target of total financial self-sufficiency and to urge Canada Post to extend the principle of industrial democracy in the management of that Postal Service in order that it be given room to act and deliver the goods on time, and at reasonable cost to the people of Canada whom we serve.

Mir. Albert Cooper (Peace River): Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to enter into this debate on the motion that has been filed by my colleague the hon. member for Haldimand-Norfold (Mr. Bradley), a motion that a number of us have wanted to have a chance to discuss. We have certainly wanted to have a chance to look at the postal facilities in Canada.
Today I want to look at basically three areas that are of concern to people in my riding. The first would be the monopoly aspects of the postal Corporation; the second would be the reduction of services that we are experiencing; and the third would be the lack of adequate facilities in many parts of my riding.
Dealing first with the monopoly aspects of the Corporation, we know that in the past there was a historical justification for this monopoly, simply because no one wanted to deliver the mail. Today there is no longer that justification. Private firms can provide the service, and there have been changes in technology that open all sorts of horizons for the delivery of mail.
In the past that monopoly was not strictly enforced, because it could not be. There was really no legal definition of a letter

that allowed them to enforce that monopoly. That situation existed from the beginning of the postal service in Canada up until today.
Suddenly we are finding that private firms and other Governments can be competitive with the postal service in both price and service. The result of that is that the post office is now feeling a little threatened, so rather than look to improvements in service and competitiveness it has moved to expand its monopoly. How did it do that? It was in the area of redefining a letter. 1 understand that as of this morning it has decided to pull back that definition and reconsider. I am glad to see that, but certainly it is a little coincidental that it happens to be on the same day that we are going to debate that very issue. That definition was designed to close out competition and to guarantee the postal Corporation's market share, regardless of its competency or its efficiency.
If we look at the definition that had been proposed, I think we will see why. It is this:
Mailable matter in any form, the mass of which does not exceed 500 grams, whether or not enclosed in an envelope, that is intended for transmission to any destination.
That definition was obviously very broad and very sweeping. We know that there were to be some exceptions to it, but they were few. What we found with that definition was that anything that could be sent was classified as mail. One of the aspects that caused me so much concern about that and about the monopolistic attitudes of the Corporation is that those powers can be defended and implemented simply by regulation, that is by Order in Council and so on. They do not have to come before the House of Commons.
This Crown Corporation can and is, and certainly was, in the terms of that past definition, willing to show its willingness to manipulate the marketplace to its own advantage, instead of really honing itself or working to improve its competition or to improve its efficiency, and essentially to create a better opportunity for itself in the marketplace. Instead of becoming the preferred route to the preferred option, it was gambling on closing the doors and forcing out its competition. What we saw in fact was that electronic mail would come under the jurisdiction of the post office. We found that courier service charges could go up and would be at a rate three times that of first-class mail. Couriers would have to charge triple that rate. We found that hand-delivered bills, whether by a municipality or by a corporation, would become illegal. They would now have to be delivered through the post office. All of this was brought about simply by publication in The Canada Gazette, and that was considered significant notice of change. That is how that definition was brought in.
Just to get an example of how that works, I think we should take a closer look at the definition process and how it came about. The information that that definition must be changed was placed in The Canada Gazette which, I am informed, has a circulation of approximately 2,700 people in Canada out of a total of 20 million who would use the postal facilities.
The only other thing that I understand was done was that a kit was sent to the media describing these changes. There was
Supply
no kit sent to industry or to major users of the postal service. In fact, what happened is that opposition to that definition came about almost by accident. It was almost by word of mouth. It almost slipped by because there was not any great amount of publicity about it.
It would seem from that and from the previous definition that what we were going to see was that Canadians would be expected to pay inflationary prices simply to guarantee the profitability of Canada Post. We know that those cost increases are going to contribute to inflation, whether by adding costs to municipalities, to utility companies or to other corporations, because they cannot hand deliver their mail. All those things are reflected back into the spiral.
Something else that would have been affected by that definition would be the fact that we would have been looking at increased courier costs simply because there would no longer be the option of using bulk mail. They would charge for every individual envelope rather than using the bulk mail rate. Also there was to be charges on electric mail.
The defence for that definition was that Canada Post would never use the extreme power it had or the full, broad range of the definition. My question is, why in the world would they want to put it in? My question now is what kind of definition are we going to be looking at? Will it be significantly improved or will there be a bit of juggling and have much the same comeback?
These broad powers seem to be more and more a bad habit of this Government. We saw that reflected in Bill C-48 and in the National Energy Program. We see it also in Bill C-10. All the time we see the Government reaching out for power over large areas of territories and saying they will never use it. My theory is, if you don't need it, don't put it in; and if you do put it in, you are dealing with bad legislation.
The last concern I have with the monopoly approach to postal service is what it does toward eliminating competition. What happens here is very simple. If we end up in a strike situation in this country, as we have in the past, Canadians will be left in a very vulnerable position. Had the definition we had previously tabled gone through, much of that competition would have disappeared. Municipalities would not have been able to deliver their own mail. Therefore, we are left in a very vulnerable position.
I want to emphasize that I essentially grew up in the postal service in a lot of ways. My father worked in the post office virtually all his life. I know that the vast majority in the postal service are competent, efficient and hard-working. My question is, why does not Canada Post try to capitalize on those natural assets rather than try to protect its inefficiencies by going for a monopoly, increasing its territory and cutting out its competition? It should be capitalizing on what it has going for it. 1 believe it has a great deal going for it.
I want to move to the second area of concern, reduction of service. I relate that to rural Canada because in rural Canada the post office has historically had and today has a very special

November 23, 1982
Supply
significance. It has become a vehicle for virtually everything, including shopping, regular mail, magazines and so on. It has become a very large part of rural life. However, there has been a steady deterioration of service in rural Canada. Now that service will be reduced even more.
This time it is going to be reduced with a double-edged sword. The first edge of that sword is no Saturday delivery. The second is that no postal stations will be open on Saturday. That may not be particularly significant in downtown Toronto, but it is in rural Peace River, rural Grande Prairie, Valleyview, Debolt and so on. Saturday is a very significant day for our farmers. It has long been the traditional marketing day, the day when farmers come to town to purchase their parts, get their groceries and, of course, pick up their mail. Suddenly we find that generations of tradition will come to an end, all this after rural customers have been suffering delivery problems in the past. Many have been driving five, ten, 15 or 20 miles or more to pick up their mail. Now there will be no Saturday delivery and the offices will not be open on Saturday.
The third area 1 want to touch on is facilities. That certainly is a very big concern in my part of the country. Not only do we have areas without delivery, which complicates things because it creates long waiting times in post offices simply because there are no boxes, but people are forced to pick up their mail in general delivery. That again complicates the process and again there are long lines. On top of that we find that many postal stations are in a poor state of repair with little room, poor light and heat, a shortage of staff, no parking space and so on. All of this is being provided by a Crown Corporation that wants to guarantee "that all Canadians have access to a basic level of service''.
1 want to give a few illustrations of that. In the City of Grande Prairie the post office is 20 years out of date. There is a shortage of boxes, both in the physical building and in the neighbourhood surrounding the town. There have been long delays for mail because of the huge line-ups for the general delivery service and lack of facilities. That City was promised a new post office building, with construction to begin in 198283. I met with senior officials of the Crown Corporation to discuss that. I now find that it has been delayed. How long, 1 do not know. I do not yet have any answers. It could be next year or the year after. There are no specifics. That area desperately needs new postal facilities.
McLellan has a post office facility which was built as a house in 1940. It is expected there will be considerable growth in that town next year with two major industries moving in. The postal facilities are already out of date for the existing population. In the Town of Grimshaw the post office is approximately one-half the size that is required. Again improved facilities have been promised, going back three years, but still no results.
In the small community of Debolt the postal facilities are so bad that they cannot even lock the door. It does not fit. It is propped shut by cans, garbage and so on. We have a lot of promises but very little tangible action in terms of providing
facilities in rural Peace River where these facilities are so desperately needed.
Coupled with this we are now going to have a reduction in delivery service. That will cause even further delays, longer line-ups, more unsorted mail and more angry customers. Still the postal service remains intent on protecting its monopoly, protecting itself and cutting off competition. However, the problems will continue because the basic problems we are faced with are not being solved.
In his speech today the Minister gave a couple of definitions of the Crown Corporation. One was with regard to price increases. He said we have to be fair, that the price of a stamp has only gone from 17 cents to 32 cents over four years. That is still more than a 25 per cent a year increase. That is the justification of a Government which so loudly and provocatively talks about the six and five regime; it says 25 per cent is not bad.
The Minister spent a great deal of time saying that the post office is making improvements and a lot of progress. I say to him that the bottom line in improvements never comes from the manager or management, it has to come from the customer. Recently a survey was done among small businesses with regard to postal service in Canada. I understand it involved about 9,000 people. Approximately 67 per cent said there was no change in service; around 24 per cent said it was worse. Only 2 per cent said it was improved. Therefore, there is still a lot of work to do, certainly in terms of service and facilities.
We should continue to press for those improvements. I know they very much affect the riding of Peace River. It is something that I still get more mail on than almost any other issue.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism)
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to have this opportunity of expressing my views on this motion. When we hear Hon. Members of the Opposition criticize alleged reductions in postal service, it soon becomes clear that the real target of their criticism is the Government. However, in this case, they missed their target. In fact, the legislation passed by the House on April 14, 1981 was approved by all parties, and no one can deny that. Thanks to this legislation under which the Canada Post Corporation was created, Canadians have enjoyed vastly improved, more consistent and faster postal services, a better job environment and all without increasing the deficit and the burden on the Canadian taxpayer.
It would be useful to recall the objects of this Crown corporation. The reason for entrusting a corporation rather than a department with responsibility for establishing and operating a postal service is that this was an opportunity for renewing the Canadian postal system and making it a source of pride for all Canadians.
November 23, 1982

So what has Parliament asked the new corporation to do? While maintaining basic postal service, the Corporation shall improve and extend its products and services, it shall provide a standard of service that will meet the needs of Canadians and that is similar, and I emphasize this, with respect to communities of the same size, and it shall utilize the human resources of the Corporation in a manner that will both attain the objects of the Corporation and ensure the commitment and dedication of its employees to the attainment of those objects. But that is not all. There is also the requirement to do all of this while maintaining rates that are both competitive and sufficient to help reduce a very substantial deficit.
At first glance, these objects seem to be so many constraints and by the same token, impossible to achieve, but nevertheless, if we take a careful look at the Corporation's first year of existence, it is clear that Canadian postal services have already made tremendous progress. The Corporation's management is to be praised for having translated the objects defined by Parliament into a management plan. I may add that the unions were also involved in this process as well as many of those who in the past have tried to introduce changes in our postal administration. Concentrating on three main elements: service, human relations and financial self-sufficiency, this management plan, which some people are anxious to criticize-i am sure 1 do not know why-has throughout 1982 given us a level of postal service we have not experienced for some time. I realize that much remains to be done, but the fact is that the Corporation is off to a head start and has a very good chance of being a winner.
The Canada Post Corporation has made service its number one priority. Service has not been interrupted. In fact, we have consistently had better and better quality service. There seems to be an atmosphere of openness in contacts between the Corporation and the unions representing its employees. Here again, Mr. Speaker, the Corporation has become more reliable as an enterprise, and less susceptible to work stoppages whenever there is a difference of opinion between parties in the collective bargaining process. The Corporation has managed to cut spending substantially without resorting to massive lay-offs that would have raised an already high unemployment rate during our present economic recession. The Corporation's objectives have all been met, and it is surprising to hear people talking about reductions in service, while the opposite is true. Keeping a steady course while at the same time keeping all three objectives in line is no mean feat, and it should be recognized that both directors and employees of the Corporation are doing an excellent job.
The question is, where was the Corporation to get the money it needed to improve services, while it had to reduce its deficit of $200 million or $300 million? How could it maintain industrial peace when it had to change many of its procedures, which would inevitably result in major changes as far as the employees were concerned? The objects that formed the basis for this new Crown Corporation were and still are essential to
Supply
the renewal of our postal service. A start has been made, and it is a fact that the infant is in pretty good health, Mr. Speaker.
If Canada's postal service is to maintain the course set out for it by the Members of this House, the Corporation's directors must have the authority to make adjustments to the manner in which, services are provided. The Corporation must be given the tools it requires to carry out its mission. The Corporation's board of directors has specific powers with a view to managing Canadian postal services. Although, as in other areas, Parliament must maintain a healthy vigilance, it would be unfortunate and contrary to the spirit in which the legislation was passed to make this debate some sort of trial based on incomplete and biased evidence.
Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that thanks to the provisions of our legislation, the objectives of the Corporation and the professionalism of its directors and its employees, Canadians will be provided with a better postal service. We have already witnessed a promising initial step. This is a start, it should be encouraged, and Members on both sides of the House should be prepared to do so.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to be able to take part in the debate on this motion by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Haldimand-Norfolk (Mr. Bradley), which states:
That this House, recognizing the importance of providing efficient, affordable, equitable mail service to all Canadians, and recognizing that Canada Post has reduced service while increasing its rates, condemns the Government for its failure to enforce the provisions of the Canada Post Corporation Act which require Canada Post to provide Canadians with adequate service at a reasonable cost.
I have had the privilege of serving as a Member of our Party's post office committee for a number of years, Mr. Speaker. I also had the distinct privilege of serving under the former post office critic, the Hon. Walter Dinsdale, who, as we are all aware, is being buried this afternoon in his home town of Brandon. Walter had a special and wonderful way of communicating with those with whom we had considerable differences.
As we are aware, the post office had, 1 believe, 28 unions and it was hoped that with this new Canada Post Corporation that number would be reduced, thereby reducing the possibility of strikes. I recall when we were meeting with the unions, in particular with CUPW, we had to deal with that flamboyant Scotsman, Joe Davidson, and Walter was able to reason with him, and then later on with Jean-Claude Parrot. 1 see the former Postmaster General smiling. Mr. Parrot was not as easy to deal with, nor as flamboyant, as the great Joe Davidson but he was a pretty tough nut, too. I also recall the many meetings we had with the Letter Carriers' Union and Bob McGarry and Bill Finley. Certainly that union has been a very reasonable one. Let us hope that both unions are now well aware of the serious situation with which the Canada Post

November 23, 1982
Supply
Corporation is faced, although I think all Members would agree that CUPW is still not the most popular union on the ratings scale across Canada.
Now, we on this side of the House had long urged the conversion of the then post office to a Crown Corporation. We were moving in that direction in 1979. I can only say, therefore, what a crushing disappointment it has been to us all to see the direction which the new Corporation, launched with such hope so short a while ago, has now taken. Years ago the Royal Mail moved swiftly, surely, efficiently and cheaply. It operated as a virtual monopoly because it did its job so well that it was unchallenged. People trusted the post office. They had such confidence in it that they paid it the ultimate compliment; they took it for granted. They did not even consider the possibility that articles in its care might be lost, delayed or damaged, things that we assume will happen today and do happen today.
I do not want to suggest that we felt its conversion to Crown corporation status would magically bring back the good old days; far from it. But we felt by providing a corporate framework, semi-autonomous from the cold hand of the cabinet, with a thrust into the icy waters of the competitive world of private enterprise, that we were giving it the best chance to work out its own salvation. So far it has not worked, for a number of reasons.
In my estimation, Mr. Speaker, the root cause of the Corporation's difficulties is the mandate with which this Government cast it adrift in the first place. Specifically, what other Crown corporation has ever been created and then told, concurrent with efforts to get its feet firmly planted in a new environment, to eradicate a massive operating deficit? It had been saddled with that deficit, 1 might add, by policies of the very Government that was wishing it bon voyage. So as the direct result of an insane repayment schedule the Government sends it off with a little christening gift of a 76 per cent increase in postal rates.
Everyone in the country, it seemed, was highly upset but the duplicity had worked; they were not upset at the Government, who had not only authorized the new rates but by its policies had made them necessary. No, they were upset at the new postal corporation. What a parting gift from its loving parent!
As a result of the framework within which it was forced to act from the very beginning, the Corporation was forced to take some very hard and unpleasant decisions. The most unsavoury of these is its quest for a monopoly in its area of operations. The very idea is repugnant in a society which likes to think of itself as still retaining some semblance of free enterprise orientation. This organization has been declared to be a genuine corporation, just like in the private sector. It has been sent out into the world with an utterly unconscionable price increase, the likes of which no private sector entity would ever be able to impose. Then, to prevent the public from registering its disapproval in the time-honoured free enterprise way, its competition is forced to charge three times whatever Canada Post charges, whether or not it is necessary from a business standpoint. Whatever Canada Post chooses to charge,
the competition is forced to price itself out of the market. It is breath-taking. It is what Karl Marx warned us about, only he thought it would be the private sector that tried taking the ordinary people to the cleaners.

speechtext: You were at the committee and voted for it.
