speechtext:
Most certainly I was at the committee, and we felt anything would be an improvement. Certainly I voted for it along with other members of the committee, but we felt the Corporation would be an improvement and we were guaranteed by the Postmaster General that it would solve a great many of the problems. I would like the Hon. Minister to refute that.
When the rest of the business community, Mr. Speaker, must compete for the patronage of the public by offering better service and greater value for money paid, I find it offensive that a Crown corporation can effectively legislate its competition out of business. The Minister, when queried in committee about couriers, sort of sidestepped the issue a bit and then finally said that, well, couriers would be tolerated. Of course, we now know they are being tolerated but this is certainly going to change, I understand. It is interesting, Mr. Speaker, that in today's Toronto Sun there is a heading which says: "McGill Prof Says Feds Show: Anti-combines Flaw". It goes on to mention the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and amendments to the Combines Investigation Act, and then finishes off with this:
The Government is one of the biggest offenders in competition, he adds. "Canada Post (run by Michael Warren) is a case in point. In mail delivery, would-be competitors are warned off by the prospect of fines and jail sentences."
We are well aware that a good many municipalities are feeling the pinch because of the great demands on their services and, of course, municipal taxes have been increasing drastically. Some municipalities are endeavouring to save money by haying their water or hydro bills, and even their tax bills, delivered by members of their staff. In my village of Burks Falls a good many bills are delivered along the main street within a few minutes, just by handing them to the people concerned. Canada Post Corporation is trying to take this matter to court because it wants to extract its pound of flesh and its 30 cents for every bill. I hope something can be worked out so that the municipalities can continue to save money in this way.
There is no problem with the small rural post offices because anything within their radius of operations is delivered within 24 hours and sometimes even less. It is when monstrosities such as the Gateway or South Central termini and the huge sorting depots in other metropolitan areas are involved that the problems begin.
I find it rather threatening that the Government sees nothing wrong in permitting this kind of competition, and I find it frustrating that by deliberate actions it has made it necessary for the municipalities to take such steps. Years ago
November 23, 1982

there was no thought of such a thing. Bills went to the post office and were delivered at nominal cost.
There is another aspect to this matter of monopoly which I find worrisome, Mr. Speaker, and that is that in the event of a postal strike, the monopoly is not lifted. That gives not only the Canada Post Corporation but the postal unions a stranglehold on the Canadian economy. Is that what the House wants? It is not what I want and it certainly is not what the businessmen and citizens of Parry Sound-Muskoka want. We are all aware of the tragic strikes that have taken place in the past. One lasted 48 days, bankrupted a good many firms and imposed a great financial burden on others.
The Post Office Corporation has announced that rates are to be increased by two cents on February 15. To add contempt to the offence, the press releases announcing this increase were actually being distributed while the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was using postal rates as an example of Government restraint, in one of his famous fireside chats. If governments were elected on the basis of gall instead of competence, the present one would be all but unbeatable. On the other hand, if they were elected on the basis of competence instead of smoke and mirrors, it would long since have gone the way of the United Reform Party, the Bloc Populaire and the Liberal Progressives.
Counting the 13 cent baby bonus with which it was launched then, that means that the Canadian public will have been asked to pay postal rate increases of over 88 per cent in less than a 16-month period.
Six and five is a big laugh, Mr. Speaker. The Canadian public is not blind. It knows full well that in times of inflation, prices will rise. All it asks is a little something in return. It asks for increased productivity.
To put it even more bluntly, it asks for better service. Canada Post Corporation officials trot out all kinds of statistics to show that, indeed, the service is getting better. They tell us that 88 per cent of mail, or whatever the current figure is, is delivered on time. Of course, no one has ever defined what "on time" really means. From the standpoint of the businessmen in my area in particular, it is easy to suspect that the definition of "on time" is being adjusted, rather than the service being improved. What we see from Huntsville, or from Burks Falls, is an average 11-day delivery time for a newspaper from there to Ottawa. We see the cancellation of rural Saturday deliveries and a bare-faced attempt to do away with Saturday wicket service as well. We now have a five-day rural mail delivery service. As has been mentioned by my colleagues, a great many farmers make it a point to go to town on Saturday and may want to register a letter or buy a money order. If the wicket service is reduced to five days, it will mean a hardship on them.
I hope that the Postmaster General will look at this aspect of postal service again. He should tell his colleague, Michael Warren, to keep his cotton-picking paws off closing small-town post offices on Saturday. He has done enough damage already by taking away Saturday delivery.
It is also worth mentioning that when the Prime Minister assumed office, the first-class postal rate was six cents. By the
Supply
standards the Government has set in its management of the rest of the economy, I suppose a 553 per cent increase in rates in 15 years is not out of the way; but it is by the standards of every other Canadian Government in history. In return we have a service that, if it did not affect the profitability of every other business in the country, would be a joke.
By profession I am a real estate broker and insurance agent. In all truth, Mr. Speaker, I can tell you that today no one would expect an offer to purchase to be put in the mail and delivered within a reasonable time. They are all sent by special courier. My sons, who now operate the business as I no longer participate in it, have their salesmen drive 100 or 200 miles to deliver an offer. All across the country insurance offices no longer depend on the post office but use a regular insurance courier. The mail is picked up at the offices and delivered to Toronto within 24 hours. If it were sent through the post office, who knows how long it would take?
These are the things that worry a great many people, Mr. Speaker. Of all the Departments of Government, this is the one about which Members receive most complaints. Weekly newspapers carry advertisements complaining about the post office. When I found out that it took 11 days for delivery of the newspapers, I wrote to one paper asking it to make sure the papers were mailed on the date which appeared on the masthead. Most newspapers are sent out on a Wednesday. I checked with the post office and found that they are sent out in bags on the Wednesday but take 11 days to travel 250 miles.
I have received letters and petitions from groups of senior citizens who are incensed by the proposed two-cent increase in the cost of mailing a letter. Many other constituents have written about delays in delivery and damaged letters.
We expect much better service than this, but it does not seem that we are getting it. The motion presented today by my hon. colleague should induce the Government to pay attention to this very important service. We hope that the Canada Post Corporation will try to do a better job in the future than it has in the past.

I think every Hon. Member of the House has been subjected to some kind of lobby with respect to this sort of

November 23, 1982
Supply
delivery, because obviously municipalities are concerned about costs and whether or not the extra two cents or indeed the current 30 cents will create problems for them.
By the same token, it seems to me that Elon. Members opposite are suggesting that a decision has been taken to reject all submissions made by municipalities and all those made by utility companies. 1 do not believe that could be further from truth. The Hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka must know that indeed discussions were entered into which would permit some flexibility and would in fact understand, recognize and permit a mechanism whereby the delivery of such mail could take place in a preferred way. I am sure the Hon. Member for Haldimand-Norfolk must be aware of the new teleprinter technology which would allow a gas meter operator to go from home to home delivering a bill to the occupant. In recognition of this, an agreement has been reached with the postal Corporation to provide for the use of this new technology. To suggest today that there is total inflexibility, that in fact a monopoly is being sought, and that there is no possibility for relief from additional pressures of added cost, quite frankly is not correct.
1 am sure my hon. friends would want me to put those comments on the record, particularly if they were not aware of them.
Whether these comments take a bit of the sting out of what they attempted to say today or whether it changes the complexion of what the Hon. Member is trying to do with his motion, I do not know, but there is no question that these comments had to be put on the record. I, for one, am particularly pleased to have been able to respond to constituents such as the Union Gas Company that have written to me and entered into negotiations directly with the postal Corporation. They are finding that it is not a great monolith, unprepared to listen to them, but is prepared to respond to the recommendations of private entrepreneurs. In fact, they are finding that the Government and the Corporation can meet their demands and concerns.
I should like to spend a few moments looking at the motion before the House, specifically as it deals with service improvement or the lack thereof, according to the Hon. Member. If the world were perfect and we had all things, I suppose all of us could have voted to have the new postal Corporation somehow wipe out all its debt, to continue to deliver mail at the rate which created the debt, to improve its service and
profile as well as the reliance upon the Corporation which people should have. I suppose we could have indicated that if it proved itself we would give it an increased rate, but this is not the kind of world in which we live. The House voted to send the postal Corporation its mandate. The time not to do it was when we had the vote. It is too late today to say that we voted to do it but we really did not want to, that we were kind of forced to and thought things would be better. I cannot accept such reasoning. We all voted as reasoning persons. We recognized that indeed we were imposing a great difficulty upon the postal Corporation, but we asked it to deal with its debt. It seems to me that Canada Post is dealing with it reasonably and that it is continuing to try to provide a service. Also it seems to me that we are not asking for the payment of that service by very difficult and expensive methods or in a disproportionate way.
If we asked people in the remote areas of Canada to pay the true cost of the delivery service, which I agree they have the right to expect, would they use it or be able to pay for it? Does it not seem reasonable that if we are to demand a service in remote areas, the beneficiaries of mail delivery elsewhere should somehow be required to pay for a portion of the cost of remote distance delivery?
In addition, I ask Hon. Members whether they truly believe that there has not been an improvement in service. After only a few months of officially gaining its status as a Crown Corporation, a status which permits Canada Post to operate as a business and without the trammels imposed by several Government Departments, it announced that 74,751 new homes and businesses across Canada would be served by some 170 additional letter carriers. Many of these calls became operational by April 1 of this year. This increased service represented the first major expansion of mail delivery service since the Government tightened financial controls in 1978-79. The improvement in mail delivery represented a $5.5 million investment in the provision of faster and more accessible mail services.
I and many Members of the House argued with some validity that there were many areas in our constituencies that by any criteria deserved increased service. At the same time we argued that somehow it had to be found within the confines of restraints. This was done. To argue today that this is not an increase in service, which should be lauded as having been accomplished by the postal Corporation, is not to acknowledge what has truthfully taken place.
The expansion of mail delivery took place right across Canada. It was not isolated to only one or two communities. Also it took place with due regard for the public purse, and the financial bottom line is a key to further progress in the mails. Canada Post's No. 1 priority is to improve service; 1 think the chairman of the Corporation indicated that. Its aim is to provide a service second to none in the mails.
Accordingly, one of the first things it did once it became a Corporation was to set up six action programs called "quick starts". It staffed teams with some of its best managers and
November 23, 1982

told them to attack immediately six critical areas where Canada Post had to intervene quickly in straightening out operations and moving the mails more expeditiously. These quick starts have paid off handsomely in boosting over-all performance.
I should like to offer Hon. Members some evidence as to where they have started to pay off. A user's guide for large volume mailers was produced and distributed. By working more closely on pre-sort and make-up requirements, Canada Post now saves time and money, which is reflected throughout the system. A turnaround team dealing with mis-sorts and mis-sends has been auditing 371 mechanized plants and postal stations. Quality control teams are checking very carefully to ensure that these miscues are corrected as quickly as possible.
Several new transportation routes have been set up to move the mail faster between high density centres. If the mail movement between my constituency and Ottawa, for example, is any test of whether or not this is working, then I have to suggest that it is.
These initiatives and others are all directed by a special body called the Service Improvement Group. It has taken over the implementation of the quick start programs and it has been charged with the responsibility of seeing that the work continues on schedule.
Canada Post also set up another group that combines senior executives from both marketing and operations to tap the ideas of first-line supervisors and managers. Canada Post was swamped with letters and memos from its own employees who really want to contribute to service improvements. They are sending in their ideas, and management is acting on many of them.
Let me cite a few specific examples of changes that are now taking place. In Calgary, a special project team is improving delivery times for processing mail from large volume mailers. In Vancouver, Canada Post adjusted the times when letter boxes are cleared to provide earlier processing at the plant. Parcel delivery in Edmonton has been reorganized, improving service by about 25 per cent. In Quebec, Canada Post redesigned some of its special delivery routes. It is beginning to improve performance in mail going to the western part of that Province. In the Atlantic postal region, sales territories have been redrawn to ensure maximum sales initiatives at minimum cost.
All of these initiatives, the quick starts, the longer term projects and the response they have generated from managers, have given the Corporation a good beginning. Canada Post is moving on a wide front, and its success so far is due to many people working a little harder or a little more smartly to improve service. Canada Post will not become a success overnight, which I do not think any Member expected, but I believe that the turnaround has begun. I suggest that the evidence is there for all of us to see.
During the past year, Canada Post has also decided to take on its most formidable competitors in the courier business. Exploiting its great advantage of having more outlets than
Supply
most, 8,000 across the country, Canada Post expanded Priority Post, its premier courier service, in major cities across Canada. Businesses are learning that important mail can and will be delivered on time and reliably. Canada Post takes pride in the growing success that this premium courier service is enjoying.
Incidentally, I might just tell the House that only last week, one of my constituents who was leaving the country and required his passport very quickly, requested-not because he particularly distrusted Canada Post but because he wanted to ensure quick delivery-that a specific courier, whom he named, be used to have his passport delivered from my constituency office. The fact is that the courier service on which everyone relied lost the passport, and we were required to do special duty in order to obtain another passport for him.
This just proves that notwithstanding the fact that far fewer pieces are sorted and delivered by that courier service, they also have miscues, misdirections and misdeliveries. It is unreasonable to expect that there will not be these misadventures.
When one looks at the number of pieces that Canada Post has to deal with each year versus the number of pieces that, in fact, do get misdirected, I do not think that any reasonable person can do anything but suggest that Canada Post is doing a very good job. I want to stand here and compliment them for what they do right, while recognizing that they are also there to receive my complaints when they do something wrong and, better still, are prepared to correct it.
Let us examine the performance of the less esoteric types of mail that almost every Canadian receives or sends out. Since becoming a Crown Corporation in October of 1981, Canada Post has focused most of its efforts on its top priority, which is to improve postal service to its customers. Changes in mail handling procedures, new transportation routes and improved controls over the national networks are just a few of the service initiatives that have been and are being applied. Consider the results of these initiatives. For August, 1982, on time delivery of first class mail was 88.7 per cent, compared with 80.4 per cent in the same period in 1980. This represents the highest monthly average that Canada Post has attained since 1976. It is true that we would like to see figures of 95 per cent or 98 per cent, but the fact is that there has been some improvement. I suggest that this proves my point that the suggestion in today's motion that there has been no improvement in services does not reflect what in fact has been happening.
Local first class mail, letters mailed within a city for delivery within the same area, had a success rate of 94.6 per cent. Forward first class mail, letters mailed for delivery in a different city, improved by 13 points. In most of the other areas sampled, mail service showed a substantial improvement over the levels of the previous year. I wonder whether, if other private sector corporations had shown that type of improvement in productivity and delivery of their goods or service, they would not just be a little proud of that and also somewhat concerned about critics still saying that they are doing it wrong.

November 23, 1982
Supply
Indisputably, Canada Post's performance has improved, is improving and shows every sign of continuing to improve. Improvement means change, and this is not brought about by the fainthearted. Daring and refreshing changes are taking place in Canada Post, which accounts for the mails being moved more expeditiously and with greater dispatch.
The new mail handling techniques are not the only explanation for improved mail delivery. Not only has Canada Post taken a fresh look at how to improve service and productivity, but smoother and more cordial labour relations are leading to a new pride among the 60,000 employees. They are beginning to realize that they belong to a class organization that is vital to the economic well-being of the nation and vital to the strength of its social fabric. A renewed pride and spirit is not the least of Canada Post's achievements and performance over the past year.
Let me reassure you, Mr. Speaker, that despite progress and achievement, Canada Post has not become smug. It fully realizes that innumerable challenges lie ahead, that only unstinting daily efforts by both management and labour can bring about a truly superlative mail service. That is the aim of the Corporation, to provide a truly superlative mail service that does not rely on the public purse. Even though the results still fall short of the standards set by the Corporation, it is clear that the revitalizing of this essential national service is well under way.
Canada Post has also made a commitment to the public and to the House. It will continue to release reports on mail service, such as the one I cited above, on a regular basis regardless of the results. I think that reflects a lot of confidence in the future by this Corporation.
The survival of Canada Post as a business is not just a concern about daily operational realities. Canada Post, while it has entered the space age, still has to look at the mails of the future. It is well aware that this is the age of the microchip and electronic wizardry that is revolutionizing communications everywhere. Canada Post recently established a business development division which is keeping the Corporation attuned to the latest developments in technology.
Canada Post is also well aware of the fact that it has to reposition its parcel services and to explore all the avenues opening up in electronic mail. It realizes that it has to find new ways to better use its more than 8,000 branch offices if it is to increase revenues substantially.
Canada Post is examining the introduction of a proof of delivery feature to telepost messages. Incidentally, telepost is that electronic mail service operated jointly with CN and CP Telecommunications. This proof of delivery feature would provide accurate records without sacrificing efficiency. The Corporation is also studying ways of providing a two to three hour delivery service across Canada to the approximately 50 communities where telepost facilies exist.
I must refer to Canada Post's approach in expanding its business and improving its performance. It has adopted the attitude that it must aggressively compete in the marketplace
for more business and revenue. This attitude that it must be aggressive and competitive underlies the record of increasing success that I have mentioned before. While some Members may hark back to the golden age of perfection in the mails, Canada Post knows full well that in terms of superior performance it cannot go forward unless it adopts the methods and attitudes of its most formidable competitors.
In conclusion I might suggest that some of my questions are addressed to that stance. I think much of what is at stake here is a continuation of the universal mail service in Canada. Such universal mail service is jealously guarded by governments of all countries, and it gives one pause to wonder just a bit why, in fact, this particular Government and this particular country should be different.
Canada Post has often been criticized with the same adjectives that are used to criticize business. 1 consider that to be a sign that the mails are now operating as a business, and 1 welcome it. Such criticism augurs well for the future of improved mail performance in Canada.

I had prepared a long dissertation in opposition to exactly what that definition said, but, hopefully, it will not be required. We have all heard the little, old adage:
A tisket, a tasket
A brown and yellow basket,
1 sent a letter to my love
But on the way the post office lost it-
And it cost me 30 cents.
We have all experienced this on a regular basis. In my offices, both here and in my riding, I personally get more mail with regard to the faulty post office service than with regard to any other item which crosses my desk.
In October of last year, when the Canada Post Corporation came into being, the president of the new corporation, Michael Warren, listed three goals for the following five years. The first was the aim of having the mail delivered on time. I am sure he said that with tongue in cheek. Second was the plan to place the Corporation in a financial break-even position. That was the first time I had ever heard of anyone who wanted to run a corporation and just make it break even. That is not the way the free enterprise system works, in my view. I just received a letter the other day which stated:
Dear Ron:
Here's another little s-disturber for you. I certainly wouldn't mind paying the postage in Canada if we had the service. The last letter I received from Bruce took three weeks. It used to take a week. We get one down here in five days.
That letter came from Florida with a U.S. postage stamp. Mr. Warren said that the second plan was to break even. I might add that the clipping which was attached to the letter came from a Florida newspaper, the Sun-Sentinel, dated November 3, 1982 and the by-line is Los Angeles. It states:
The U.S. Postal Service made money in fiscal 1982 and a postal rate increase projected for late 1983 will be put off until 1984, Postmaster General William Bolger said.
Letters in the United States require only a 20 cent stamp, yet the U.S. post office makes a profit. That is a little different from what we are asked to accept here by Mr. Warren. Third, he hoped to establish a closer relationship with the Corporation's eight unions. I am sure that every person in Canada wishes him well and, as has been pointed out by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling), both with CUPE and some of the others, he has his work cut out for him, but we do wish him well. These goals of efficiency and self-sufficiency were admirable, but right from the beginning it was recognized that the attainment of these aims would result in internal upheaval and in additional financial burden on the users of the postal service, because when costs outrun revenues by that much, then things do not run on time and service must suffer. Thus, the fact that both these problems have surfaced should come as no surprise to any of us.
What has been a surprise, a most unwelcome surprise, I might add, and an unwarranted one at that, is that the factors contributing to the creation of these problems led to a reduction and not an expansion of the existing services as was expected. We are now paying more for something and getting
Supply
less. We are paying First World price for service, but we are getting Third World class in service.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext: That's not your quote.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext:
Mail delivery on Saturday, in rural areas, which is considered an important and vital service to those involved, has been eliminated. Despite official claims that on time delivery of first class mail has improved, senders and receivers right across the country, and everyone who spoke here have a litany of horror stories. We all know better than to think that service has been expanded. News stories of mail taking days to reach its destination in the same city remain frequent and have led to public frustration, and the continuing annoyance and anger of the public is not without substance. Proof of this attitude can be found in the Corporation's own figures which reveal that the usage of the service has dropped noticeably. Canadians who had expected improvements and should have seen improvements, have now had their hopes dashed again and, in disgust, have turned to alternative services where possible.
What has been the Corporation's response to those defections? It chose to legislate rather than to entice. It sought to expand upon its monopoly rather than to improve its service. I hope this announcement will give the Corporation its second sober thought that we hear so much about. It has sought to expand its monopolies rather than improve its services, and then it redefined "a letter" which we have already gone through.
That redefinition of "a letter" upsets so many Canadians that it actually alienated them even further, and the response to this arbitrary definition was predictable. Strong and angry opposition was heard from the financial community, from business, consumer groups, the municipalities and the public in general. The Minister responsible for Canada Post, who is seated across the aisle, has received over 300 representations since the last I heard, and I would bet there are many more by today, concerning the complete matter. Therefore, there could have been no doubt in the minds of Government Members opposite when this was brought to their attention today that they had better do something about it, and do it quickly.
The first intimation that the Corporation was looking to grab extra bucks where it could, came when the proposed definition of "a letter" was published in the Canada Gazette on July 3. The public was given 60 days to respond, as we are aware, and will now have 60 more days. This is the first time since the issue came to public attention in over four months that the Government has had the decency to respond, prompted, I presume, by today's opposition. Only today, when forced to speak to the issue because the Official Opposition selected the topic for debate, did the Minister responsible for the Corporation finally get around to ending the form and climate of uncertainty which has existed since the definition was announced. It has taken the Government four months to come to its senses and agree not to support this disastrous definition. I wish it had done the same with regard to metric.

November 23, 1982
Supply
For this tardy yet welcome response, we can be grateful. However, the Minister has stated that the Government itself will be bringing forward its own regulations on the issue some time in the spring. Knowing the Government's penchant for dipping into people's pockets on even the barest pretext, I am not so sure that the Government's own definition of "regulations governing the Corporation's mandate" will not result in an equally odious proposal. Let us hope not.
It is to be hoped that the Government will take serious note of the obligations raised over the definition of "a letter" when it begins to form its own rules. It should pay attention to the fact that the business community has taken strong exception to any further penalties being placed on it in connection with the use of courier services. In the case of my own business, I would have had to break the law to continue to deliver my statements of account to my customers. The business community is absolutely beleaguered by a chaotic economic climate, and it relies on rapid transit of its transactions to remain current and solvent. There seems to have been no consideration of that fact taken into account. In the absence of reliable public postal service, many businesses have turned to private couriers for this vital asset of their operations. The Government, when creating the Corporation, was aware that if it banned couriers or made their use prohibitive, it would face an absolutely embarrassing revolt by business. All the letters we have received have affirmed that. Therefore, couriers were permitted to operate, but it was stipulated that the fee involved had to be at least three times the cost of sending a letter by mail, which has been pointed out by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka. The fact that thousands of Canadian businesses chose to accept this exhorbitant rate, rather than use the mail, attests to their lack of confidence in the postal service. The Corporation, with its back to the financial wall, instead of improving service to entice such users back into its fold, sought to further penalize those who out of necessity turned to other services.
Now we come to the matter of electronic transmission, which I am sure must come up again. While electronic mail is exempt during transmission, the proposed definition which we had before us appeared to mean that once a paper copy of the transmission had been made, the paper copy was then considered a letter, and postage had to be paid. Absolutely idiotic. Anyone could realize instantly just what was happening, and what a financial nightmare this would become, for businesses to have to pay for services that were not rendered. One wonders about the mentality responsible for this type of thinking. It reminds me of the metric issue. The Government was right finally to refuse to accept such a dumb definition of a letter. I wish that they could reconsider the metric question.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext:
The refusal was appropriate on many counts, not the least of which was the regulation involving punishment for non-compliance. Mandatory definition of a letter at this point, mandatory use of metric, and the threat to Canadians of
something not debated properly in the House of Commons, not gone to committees, is the threat of imprisonment. That is something we have to keep in our minds, that by Order in Council it is legal now in the wonderful country of Canada to have internment camps.
There was a provision which stated that any violator could be prosecuted by indictment or summary conviction and given anything from a fine to five years in prison. Is that not really something for us to believe in that in this country of Canada you could actually get a prison sentence for violating such a simple thing as a letter. It is interesting to note that any time the Government or its agencies introduce new legislation it seems, lately, there is always inserted that threat of imprisonment. This is quite possibly one of the reasons why the Government laid the groundwork for the establishment of internment camps under the Emergency Measures Order, as it was passed by Order in Council.
This Government is becoming famous, or infamous, as the case may be, for threatening to put Canadians in jail if they do not do what the Government orders. Mandatory imposition has become the rule, not the exception. Canadians do not deserve to be behind bars. The people who consider that they had to use that threat maybe should take their place.
The very fact that the regulation was proposed in the first place should indicate to the Government that something is terribly wrong with the direction being implemented by senior officials of Canada Post. The goals I first reiterated are commendable. The methods being used to obtain those goals are not.
There was a time when mail delivery in Canada was the envy of other nations around the world. The words, "Royal Mail", on trucks, street boxes, uniforms and buildings seemed to signify a type of treatment being given the transmission and delivery of letters and parcels. For a few pennies at most, our mail was delivered swiftly and intact. The post office then had a well-deserved reputation. I worked as a postman at Christmastime, as a youth in high school, and as a summer job, and I know how important that oath was to all of us and how we would scamper all over that post office when we could not ascertain where a letter should be delivered, to make sure that it got to its rightful owner. The "Royal Mail" was given "royal" attention. Why do we then find ourselves in the mess we are in today?
It is perhaps no coincidence that our sorry lapse into the present state of affairs began when this Government, in an effort to stamp out all references to the word "royal", included the Post Office in its fevered and foolish rush to establish a hyphenated Canada as the questionable mark of our national and independent identity. Small wonder, then, that the Government exhibits no alarm over the arrogance of Canada Post officials. When you abandon tradition, you also turn your back on the values such tradition engenders. These values, and the result of attempts to live up to such values, provided the nation with services in many areas which were second to none. The handling of our "royal" mail was a prime example. When the
November 23, 1982

Government eliminated the word "royal it seemed to signal an abandonment of the type of service implicit in the word.
Thrust into the void, Canada Post has created new types of service, priority post, intelpost and telepost, all designed simply to generate more money for the Corporation not better service, only more money.
The price increase in stamps is the next thing 1 would like to look at for a moment. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) came to office stamps were 6 cents. At the end of 1981 the price rose to 30 cents a stamp, up from 17 cents, an increase of 88 per cent. We did not get a corresponding increase in the quality of service. Another increase, to 32 cents, is set to take place this coming February 15. We have four more years to go before the goal of self-sufficiency is achieved. You don't have to be a mathematician to realize how much higher the price of postage stamps will have to go before this goal is realized. The President of Canada Post has said that the next increase would have been much higher, but he was forced to remain within the Government's six and five guidelines. In the meantime I understand Great Britain's post office is running at a profit, and you have just heard that the United States is actually postponing a price increase.
Two years down the road the President of Canada Post will undoubtedly find a way to make up for the loss resulting from the period of imposed restraint. By that time the five or six people left using the service will be faced with a postage stamp worth more than the dollar it costs to buy it. Mr. Warren is not worried, why should he be? No single person, in my view, is worth a salary of between $100,000 and $150,000, who does not generate productivity. I would suggest that if Mr. Warren wants to be a winner he should set aside his personal goal and give his undivided attention to the manner in which he pursues the three goals which he stated for the Corporation.
In Hansard on July 19, 1982, at page 19439, under Standing Order 43, I was referring to the difficulty of mail delivery to one of my constituents. The suggestion I made then was that the cost of each registered letter not delivered within 48 hours be deducted from the salary of the President of Canada Post, and perhaps he would recognize the plight of Canadians with regard to their postal service. That still stands.
Relations between Canada Post employees and management have deteriorated to a point of almost constant confrontation, and the public has borne the brunt and the cost of this conflict. To dwell on the labour-management issue at this point would serve no purpose. The issues of contention are well documented and widely known. What we are looking for are answers and improvements.
By implementing policies which would create confidence in the service, by delivering the mail on time and intact, the management of Canada Post and its employees would certainly earn the respect of Canadians. To ask this Government to appreciate the necessity of public respect is perhaps asking too much. The Post Office, on the other hand, was once a respected institution. I would suggest to officials that too much time
Supply
and effort has been wrongly directed to the definition of a letter, and that in the ensuing time that we have, when this goes back for a change, that it be struck from their minds.
I would further suggest that they study very carefully the dictionary definition of "service". The Oxford Dictionary tells us that service is the work done to meet a need. The need exists. I defy any Member of this House to go out on the street tonight and ask 20 Canadians what they think about their post office, and to tabulate the answers and bring them back to the House.
Someone must ensure that the work to meet this need is done. That someone is this Government. Because this Government has failed miserably in its effort to provide this service, I wholeheartedly support the motion before us today.

Mr. Speaker, when in 1980 the Government finally brought in legislation which turned the Post Office from a Government Department into a Crown corporation, that proposal had almost unanimous approval from all Members of this House. That consensus came about because the experience of a dozen or more years with the Post Office being run as a Department of Government was so bad that the public and Members of Parliament recognized that a very drastic and fundamental change would have to be made.
What were the reasons of the decline of the popularity of the Post Office? There was, of course, a tremendous increase in the amount of mail which the Post Office was called upon to move. The Government decided on the advice of some so-called experts that the way to handle this tremendous increase was to mechanize and computerize the system. Instead of trying the new system in a smaller city to find out whether and how it worked, the Government installed the new system in the Toronto area where 40 per cent of all mail originates.
It was several years after the computerized system was installed before all the bugs were found and the difficulties eliminated. Indeed, they may not have been eliminated until now. For a long time we had a situation where Toronto mail was shipped by truck to Peterborough to be sorted by hand, brought back to Toronto and then sent on to its destination. People became very angry. One could not blame them. They were justified in their anger, but they vented it on the wrong people. They assumed that the difficulties and failures were somehow due to the Post Office workers, when in fact they were the responsibility of management which had made such fundamental errors.
Besides that we had management backed by a Government which simply refused to deal with its employees in a twentieth century way in face-to-face discussion, looking for solutions to the difficulties and differences which arose. Over the years there were a number of strikes, some legal and some not.
A number of studies were commissioned by the Government. Judge Montpetit, Stewart Martin and several others all
reported that the difficulties were as a result of bad management practices in the Department. Then, Mr. Speaker, there was the added difficulty that the Post Office Department, and its Minister, could not negotiate with the unions. That job was given to the Treasury Board, which was always concerned about how a particular improvement or concession would affect other people. After many years it was decided that the Post Office should be transformed into a Crown corporation, and, as I said earlier, that decision was endorsed by virtually all the Members of Parliament. Our Party supported that change because we believed then, and we believe now, that it was a change which was needed. We believe that the people of Canada want and have a right to expect an efficient, affordable and equitable mail service. We consider the post office should be a national public utility supported by the people of Canada. We are dealing with the deficit by constantly increasing the price of mailing letters or magazines and newspapers. This is wrong in principle. One might as well say, Mr. Speaker, that if the people of the cities or the rural areas cannot afford to pay for health services directly, they should not have health services, and if the people of an isolated community, for example, in northern Manitoba, cannot afford to pay for the cost of teachers in their schools, they should not have schools. The delivery of mail, letters, magazines, books, newspapers, is a right of all Canadians and the cost should be borne equitably by all Canadians. The price for delivery of a letter within the City of Winnipeg should not be any higher than the price for delivering a letter to the Northwest Territories, a difference of thousands of miles, nor should the price be lower.
We recognize that as a part of the improvement in service an increase in rates was necessary, but we feel the amount of the increase since the change-over to the Crown Corporation has been unfair and violates the Corporation's duty to provide good service to all sectors of Canadian society at reasonable rates. I point out that the cost of mailing a first-class letter in Canada has risen in two years from 17 cent to 32 cents. That is an increase, Mr. Speaker, of almost 90 per cent. At the same time service to individuals has been reduced.
We have heard mention of closing some rural post offices on Saturdays, and there are rumours about a three-day service instead of five-day service, and I could go on and on. We know, for example, that letter carriers have been cut back on overtime, which means, of course, that service to individual homes is reduced. We are told it has been recommended in the post office that no substitutes be provided for sick or otherwise indisposed letter carriers. This recommendation is widely believed to be the first step toward ending the five-day delivery service and a consideration of an every-other-day delivery service.
We know that the average family who may send and receive only a few letters per week pays the highest rate as first-class mail costs go up, but the level of their service is gradually being reduced. On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, the Canada

Post Corporation is bending over backwards to encourage corporate mailing by offering more services and proportionately passing on lower rate increases for first-class service. If it were not against the rules of the House, 1 would bring into the House the mail which comes to my office, and which comes to every Member of this House of Commons every day. It would take a very large cardboard carton. And I know, as well as the Minister, that 95 per cent of the mail which we get goes into the garbage.

At the same time as they have had imposed on them a maximum 6 per cent increase in their wages, first-class mail rates have increased by over 75 per cent. Point out that first-class mail represented losses of just 23 per cent on the cost of providing service at the same time as business bulk mailing represented losses of 42 per cent for third-class mail and 130 per cent for fourth-class mail.
I would like the Minister at some time, if not today, to explain to Members of this House and the Canadian public why they should be forced to pay an increase of almost 100 per cent. I suppose within the next year we will reach or exceed the magic number of 100 per cent. At the same time, business mail, most of which is unsolicited and most of which I classify as junk mail, is showing the kind of losses and getting the kind of subsidies from the Government and the people of Canada which it does.

Mr. Speaker, in the current period the Canada Post Corporation is announcing a set of rates for corporations. Our position is that more attention should be focused on the

need of individual Canadians and small businessmen. What is a more efficient postal service? Our response would be a service which provides a basic customary postal service to the greatest possible number of Canadians, whether they live on the prairies or the far North, or an individual in northern Manitoba.
Let me digress for a moment, Mr. Speaker, to deal very briefly with some of the arguments advanced during this debate and earlier in committee when we were passing the legislation to establish the Crown Corporation.
We have the argument that the Government and the post office were being too restrictive in their definition of a letter. The argument was advanced that we should not restrict the definition of a letter; we need more competition. Those people who say that, Mr. Speaker, are doing a great disservice to Canadians, particularly to Canadians who live in the bigger cities of this country. If you got the so-called competition which some of the banks and other commercial organizations want, Mr. Speaker, you would have those organizations skimming off the easy and cheap to deliver mail in the big cities. What would be left for the post office? All the difficult mail, all the rural and isolated areas where the cost to deliver mail is very expensive. Then you would get the argument that the Postal Corporation could not afford to provide the kind of service it has been providing until now. You would get further cutbacks in service in the rural and isolated areas, as we have had cutbacks in VIA rail service. So we say that we want the post office to be efficient and able to deliver mail quickly, without the mistakes which have happened before.
However, Mr. Speaker, we do not believe that efficiency means subsidizing corporate business structure, which is interested in selling its goods by getting a subsidy from the people of Canada. We believe that a step in the right direction for the kind of program I have talked about would be a clear definition of what basic customary postal service really means.
I say to the Minister that it means, in the cities and suburbs of Canada, door-to-door delivery. It does not mean delivery to letter boxes in suburban areas which may be a mile or more from where people live. We had that situation right into the 1979 election. The fact that an election was looming is what got the Government to agree to the hiring of more letter carriers. 1 do not know whether it is going to need another election, but we need to get the kind of door-to-door service to the suburbs that the cities have had for many years. If we do, then we would have a much better basis for judging proposed cuts in delivery service, the refusal to provide home delivery in certain areas, the closing of post offices in smaller centres and outlying areas, and the increasingly inflated costs for first-class service.
That is the kind of approach we need, Mr. Speaker. What we need is for the Government and Parliament of Canada to give that kind of directive or objective to the Crown Corporation, to let them know what we expect from them. What we expect is that they meet the needs of ordinary citizens and

Mr. Speaker, I would like to address myself to a few statements made earlier in the debate by the Hon. Member for Simcoe South (Mr. Stewart) who sits across the aisle. He said that this Government will be tabling a definition of "a letter" in the very near future. The fact is that it is the Corporation which will be tabling this definition. Not only that, there will be 60 days for the public to respond. If they have any problems with the definition, then there is still time for change at that time.
The Hon. Member also said that the Cabinet is probably making a decision about the definition because of the debate taking place today. 1 suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that this is not so. The Cabinet has been having extensive consultations across Canada, and this is the latest possible time Cabinet could make the decision in order to hear all possible views and get all possible input from all the people across Canada. I would suggest in turn that it is quite possible that the Members of the Conservative Party probably chose this topic to coincide with the decision taken by Cabinet. That is a possibility, in fact even a probability.
It was also mentioned by the Hon. Member that the post office lacked flexibility. Well, Mr. Speaker, the post office has been negotiating with industry's bulk mailers, and 1 would like to read a quotation from Friday's wire services which says:
Manitoba Hydro will save about $100,000 a year because of new Canada Post Corp., rates for bulk mail, Hydro spokesman Verne Prior said Friday.
Another one from Toronto says that:
Proposed rates for bulk mailing recently approved by Canada Post Corp. could save utilities in Ontario about $2 million next year-
That is right, $2 million. You shake your head in wonderment, Mr. Speaker, and no wonder indeed because $2 million is surely nothing to be sneezed at. Charlie Macaluso, a research officer with the Ontario Municipal Electrical Association says:
I think we've developed probably one of the better understandings and cooperative arrangements with the post office ever.
That Association, Mr. Speaker, represents more than 300 of Ontario's 324 municipal utilities. Not only that, Mr. Speaker, we had people who were in times past greatly affected by the mail strikes of the post office. But now we see that the Canada Post Corporation and the greeting card industry have undertaken a joint study to look at an appropriate rate for Christmas cards for next Christmas. This recommendation will be brought forward by January, 1983 to assist the greeting card industry.
So quite contrary to what the Hon. Member was saying earlier about the inflexibility of the Post Office, I suggest to you that the Post Office indeed is adjusting to the problems of the times. It is not only giving better service for the money but is also taking greater care to ensure that the mail is being delivered on time.
I should like to address myself to the improved labour relations at Canada Post Corporation and the improved reliability of delivery of mail. The Opposition motion states that there is no proof that service has improved since the post office became a Crown corporation a year ago. 1 beg to differ. There is one very tangible way in which service has improved over 1980 and 1981.
In 1980, the Post Office suffered a two-month strike which not only crippled our Canadian postal system and sent business scurrying for emergency arrangements to move mail, but which cost the Department a loss of more than 660,000 person days. In 1981, work disruptions of various kinds, short of a general strike, cost more than 14,000 person days. In 1982, I am happy to report, there have been less than 100 person days lost through work disruptions to date.
Now, Mr. Speaker, no single factor contributes more to service deterioration than work disruptions or strikes. Therefore, we can certainly say that it is with service improvement in mind-or more precisely, with an improvement in the reliability of service-that management at Canada Post, with the support of the Government, has pursued a very creative approach to union-management relations. The purpose is to improve those relations, and the dramatic drop in person days lost through either a strike or work disruptions certainly points to the efficiency of the approach.
These improved results are not the product of a fluke. The Corporation's management set out to balance its three basic objectives of improved service, improved human relations and the achievement of self-sufficiency in such a way as to avoid situations which could escalate into work disruptions. When we consider the climate under which the Corporation is operating these days, with volume drops from the recession, wage guidelines and stressed labour relations all around, we can appreciate the delicate balancing act which is required.
The extensive cost-cutting and savings operations which Canada Post has had to pursue in order to meet its mandate which calls for a reduction of its deficit, have added a great deal of stress to the working environment. And yet, the Corporation is ending its first year of operations with a loss of less than 100 person days. I think this is a phenomenal achievement, when compared to the 660,000 person days lost in 1980.
The present situation is that about 97 per cent of employees at Canada Post are unionized, and this includes most supervisors and managers. In the last decade, the post office was the scene of some intense union-management discord. The result is that there is now a public perception that this counterproductive environment is standard operating procedure. One of the toughest jobs at Canada Post, therefore, is to follow a program which addresses the problems honestly and which works towards changing attitudes and practices. It is these attitudes and practices which must be attacked. There must be a change in the way employees and employers work, so that efficient mail delivery can be achieved.

Why the situation developed in the first place is not an easy question to answer. However, Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that the Canada Post Act, which all Members in this House supported, was meant to change past practices dramatically. I stress that virtually every Member voted in favour of establishing the Canada Post Corporation.
Until October 16, 1981, there were three employers dealing with the unions in the negotiating process at the post office. The Department of Finance, which set fiscal policy for the country and had the over-all financial mandate for negotiations; the Treasury Board, which did the bargaining and was, in law, the employer; and, finally, the post office which ran the business from day to day. Each of these three employers had different objectives and the process was, to put it mildly, awkward.
Moreover, the bargaining process was extremely formal; it was almost quasi-judicial in nature. Under the Public Service Staff Relations Act, the normal conciliation services designed to facilitate freely negotiated settlements in the private sector were not available to the post office. In their place came imposed settlements, made by arbitrators, Parliament and even the courts. Even after some of these imposed agreements, the issues often remained as points to be squabbled over within the organization.
The Corporation now can negotiate directly with labour representatives. This new climate has already affected the spirit at Canada Post. The Corporation has begun to cast off some of the counter-productive emotional baggage of previous negotiations, such as removing or brushing away the longstanding problems of cumbersome grievance procedures, salary inequities, lack of co-ordination in safety programs and other things.
The Canada Post Act gave the post office a new lease on life. It would seem that the fresh start provided by Crown status is showing some results. Certainly, Mr. Speaker, there are still a lot of problems to be resolved, but at least they are being discussed without the acrimony which leads to work disruptions and strikes.
Another example of the new atmosphere which is beginning to develop at Canada Post is that a letter of understanding was signed in January 1982 with representatives of the nearly 23,000 members of the Letter Carriers' Union of Canada.
That understanding is particularly noteworthy because under a new, more streamlined bargaining process, both parties accepted their responsibilities to settle differences together, without resorting to a third party to make the tough decisions. The understanding was reached without undue delay, because both sides recognized the implications for customers and consumers of the 1980 strike. This particular set of negotiations led to the successful introduction of productivity bargaining, a system whereby people work a little harder to get more pay.
Canada Post worked with the union to identify a variety of cost savings associated with the delivery of mail. Both parties then negotiated a sharing of these savings between the union and the Corporation. The union directed its share to financing
Supply
additional wages and benefits for its members, of course, while the Corporation directed its share to reducing the over-all cost of the settlement and helping to finance future letter delivery service improvements.
These service improvements took place, Mr. Speaker. Thousands of new homes have benefited from service where there was none before.
Productivity bargaining is a key to this and it has helped the Corporation to identify, in just this one agreement, many millions of dollars in savings that can be made over the next few years, it is therefore ironic, Mr. Speaker, that news of the best efforts of the Corporation and the Letter Carriers' Union of Canada did not reach the public. It certainly did not reach Members opposite.
Another change in the working environment which has been brought about by a creative approach to human relations is reflected in the interest employees are taking in improving service. The Corporation has already published two reports which clearly show a steady 10 per cent improvement in service for first class mail across the country over the year. Large customers have, through their own survey, confirmed this trend, as have independent businessmen. This shows that the employees at Canada Post, to use a popular phrase, are being "turned on again''. They are taking pride in their work, and we in Canada are also taking pride in their work and in our postal service. Otherwise they would not have ensured the success of the Corporation's program called "quick starts", which were designed to bring about steady service improvements.
The old structure when the post office was a department was not favourable to good human relations; neither were the internal procedures in such areas as job classification and grievances. These were frustrating and merely increased the feeling of despair among employees. When the Crown Corporation was created, the new management found that two-thirds of the huge backlog of grievances should never have left the shop floor, that is, they could have been settled by first-line supervisors and not made their way into the huge vat of stale grievances to be left to fester.
These problems are being addressed today in a whole new way. Canada Post's business plan, its first ever, lists improving human relations as a top priority. It ranks second after service, but this does not mean that it is dealt with after service has improved enough to allow management to turn its attention to it. No, both these goals along with self-sufficiency have to be addressed without faltering. Some of the rules Canada Post is using in an effort to improve the working environment are the same for any business. They boil down to dealing with people with respect, so that they, the workers, enjoy self-respect.
The Corporation is leaving behind the days when union members or leaders could think they had a right to disrupt a business for questionable goals, but it is also leaving behind practices which disregarded employees as people and treated

November 23, 1982
Supply
them merely as bodies to shift, names on a chart or merely in statistics. The stewardship of the Corporation rests with management. It cannot shirk its responsibilities, and it does not want to do so. There is also a very important ongoing dialogue with the unions, as well as a sharing of decisions with labour. This is why Canada Post Corporation has two labour leaders on its board of directors. They share in the decisionmaking and they serve to communicate to management what motivates the unionized work force.
These board members can pass on to membership in the unions the message that real job security can only come from a thriving competitive business. No business can be competitive, let alone efficient, if its life is constantly interrupted by work disruptions or by strikes. There is no job security no matter what iron-clad contracts exist if the business, that is the employer, goes under.
In conclusion, Canada Post's first business plan was prepared in consultation with all the unions. They are all aware of the Corporation's priorities. The participation of unions on the board of directors does not ensure lethargy on the part of the unions. Of course it does not, but some people tend to confuse good labour relations and the absence of strike with complete sweetness and light. This is not the case. The reality is quite different. It must be remembered that unions are political organizations as well, and that they must often be perceived by their membership as being in conflict with management to ensure their survival, in some instances. Therefore, successful bargaining is a skill. It is not something a person is born with; however, it can be learned and improved.
The real essence of the exercise is practising the art of the possible, and this is what the management of Canada Post has been doing with success, as we can see from the resulting low work stoppage figures for 1982.

I will not dwell too long on the comments of the Hon. Member for Welland (Mr. Parent). He told us that there was a dramatic improvement in shifting from the post office department to the Crown Corporation. If that is the case, it is the same as the situation where a person trades in his or her car for an Edsel. I submit that the improvement is not there, and I will give some facts to back it up. Also the Hon. Member for Welland gave a great litany of all the wonderful things happening in Canada Post. I challenge him to insert his speech in his householder to his constituency. If he is of the view that there is a great revelation, a turnaround, and that everyone is happy, I would tell him there is one person, John Bulloch, President of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, to convince. He surveyed thousands of small-business people and discovered that 64 per cent thought there was no improvement with the new Crown Corporation, 34 per cent
thought that the situation was worse, and 2 per cent thought it was better.
In early 1980 a person in Canada said, "Here come the eighties; welcome to Canada". I would like to tell the House about Canada. It is the land where the stamps lick the people rather than the other way around. We are into a situation where our mail delivery is so undependable and inconsistent- and I emphasize the word "inconsistent"-in terms of regularity of service that it simply means in some cases a cost to business at the gain of Canada Post. If this Crown Corporation were running the pony express, it would probably issue riders with sawhorses on the basis that they were efficient and that mail delivery would be as fast as it is at present.
I accept the challenge of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) this afternoon. He said that we should recognize the challenge facing Canada Post. He and others in the Government should recognize the challenge facing the Canadian business community. Approximately 30 years ago delegations from other nations came to Canada to study our postal system. They are not coming any more. Interestingly enough, by contrast, in Switzerland today any letter mailed at night is in the addressee's mailbox the next morning. People will ask, how crazy can we be to use such a comparison, recognizing that Switzerland is a small country. Anyone who knows the mountain terrain and the separation of communities in that country knows that despite its smallness, the delivery of mail up and down the mountainside is every bit as difficult if not more so than in Canada. Yet Switzerland has dependable and assured overnight delivery.
There is a six and five slogan in the country. This program applies to Canada Post as well-six days for delivery of first-class mail, on the average, and five days if one is lucky. We simply do not have an adequate, dependable system. Let us look at a number of examples. One I should like to put forward is that of a Rotary Club in my constituency which passed a motion that it should send out a little reminder notice the day before its meeting indicating that the meeting will be the next day and the name of the guest speaker. The Rotary meetings were held at noon on Tuesdays. Therefore, they wanted to depend on receiving a notice on Monday that would remind them of their Tuesday meeting. When these notices were mailed on Monday, of course they did not arrive on time. That is acceptable. They decided to back up to Friday. Again, they found that on many occasions the message did not arrive until after the meeting. Therefore they backed up once again to Thursday, only to discover that there were cases of notices not being received until the meeting was over. They decided to back up one more day, to Wednesday, but sure enough, on a regular basis there were cases of some people getting the notice the next day, on Thursday. In other words, what good is a notice on Thursday for a meeting to be held the next Tuesday?
I have given this example to explain one of the problems in the post office. Sometimes you receive brilliant service and at
November 23, 1982

other times you do not. There is no consistency in Canada Post.
Canada Post must take into consideration the fact that the success of many businesses depends upon the predictability of delivery. The situation as it concerns newspapers in the country is appalling. I had occasion to visit one of my constituents. He had a bundle of Edmonton journals on his table, and I asked him why he did not receive the newspapers. He proceeded to give me a speech about Canada Post. He said that he had not received one newspaper for a whole week and then received six newspapers in one day. What can any household do with a bundle of old newspapers after the $75 a year subscription has been paid? 1 suggest you would have an information overload if you were to attempt to read those newspapers.
The post office cannot simply make excuses for delays such as this. The fact of the matter is that the service is inadequate. That example gives us an idea of what is happening with daily newspaper delivery. This happens regularly in rural areas where subscribers do not receive papers for several days and then receive a flood of them on one day.
The same situation is true of the delivery of weekly newspapers in this country. It may take as long as ten days for a weekly paper to be delivered through the postal system. Of course this means that the newspaper is of no value as far as its announcements for the coming weekend are concerned. People in rural communities want to know when the next bingo is, and they expect to receive that information in the newspaper for which they have paid a subscription. This delay means the newspaper will only be delivered after the events have taken place.
I challenge any Member to dispute the fact that there are many publishers and editors of weekly newspapers who are complaining that they are losing subscriptions from those people who have moved away from their rural community but want to keep in contact with their home town because their papers are arriving 14 days after being mailed. That is the situation which exists with weekly newspapers being sent through our mailing system.
1 would like to talk about the costs being incurred as a result of the late deliveries in the postal system. Again, I will single out publishers. There are 22 weekly newspapers in my riding. The publishers of those newspapers are saying that they are losing advertising dollars because the advertisements arrive for printing only after the paper has been published. I am sure Hon. Members can appreciate that some of those advertisements are time-sensitive. The initial result of this delay is a loss to the advertiser. As well, there is the loss of revenue to the newspaper because it does not receive the advertising dollars, and finally there is the loss of opportunity to the person who may have wanted to take advantage of the goods and services being advertised. But what about the post office? Canada Post gets paid for its postage stamp for the mailing even though the service to the customer was nil. It gets its money while the rest in the chain end up paying. That is unacceptable.

Newspapers in the community of Provost, Alberta, leave at 4.30 p.m. for delivery in Edmonton. They arrive by bus in Edmonton at midnight on the same night. Interestingly enough, it takes approximately five days from then for delivery to homes in Edmonton to the former residents of the community of Provost. The publisher complains to the Edmonton Post Office and the answer he receives is that this is normal service. That is not acceptable service, normal or otherwise.
If we examine the whole question of what is happening in rural Canada, I submit that rural Canada is rapidly coming to the conclusion that it will no longer tolerate the condition of having to negotiate sales of $100,000 combines over party line telephones while our neighbours in the cities can have private lines for the same price. We will no longer tolerate the fact that people in the cities have cable television while television programs are beamed into the rural villages that deal only with issues in those small towns and villages, and the farmers receive the same inadequate service. Rural Canadians will no longer tolerate the fact that there is door-to-door free postal delivery in the cores of our major cities while farmers have the privilege of renting a mailbox for $12 a year so that they might have the services of Canada Post. Discrimination between rural and urban communities is unacceptable in this country on national services such as television, communications and the post office.
Even in some of our smaller communities it takes as much as 10 or 11 days for the circulation of mail. I have examples of this as well. There is no other description for the Calgary central Post Office located in my Alberta constituency but that it is outlandishly horrible. The Edmonton Post Office ranks slightly above that. I can quote one newspaper editor who recently said to me, "I can no longer rely on postal service for time-related messages." He sent for a sign in Calgary. After waiting for one month he phoned to find out where his sign was. The company manager told him that they did not have an order for a sign. Therefore, he stayed on long distance telephone and ordered his sign that way. This shows that the post office still gets paid for its stamp when the service is inadequate while that individual has to pay more and suffer the delay as well. Again, this is unacceptable.
We now have a situation where the post office tells us that we have to bag our own mail for weekly newspapers. That is not necessarily a bad idea, and most of the publishers are not opposed to it. The exception is that they even have to bag one newspaper that is to be delivered to a single subscriber in another community. The offices of these weekly newspapers are cluttered with mailbags, a situation which legitimately makes them angry. To add to this frustration, they find when, they carry these bags to the post office, that they are faced with the audacity of the postmaster saying, "We like this bag in that corner and this bag in that corner." These private entrepreneurs are in the post office doing postal work. I submit that this is an absolutely intolerable situation. There is something vitally wrong if this Crown Corporation, with the subsidies which it receives, is still calling upon people to do its work while making a profit on its unacceptable service.

I have just touched on something that I would like to express with an example. 1 said that they are making a profit on their unacceptable service, and here is the example. On October 21 of this year, a professor at Camrose College, in Camrose, Alberta, wanted a book. He ordered the book from Toronto, a great and lovely city here in central Canada. The book did not come. So, as recently as November 18, a few days ago, he phoned Toronto long distance from central Alberta, wanting to know where the book was. He was told by the company that it did not know where it was. He was told that it was shipped the same day as they received his order. He said, "I must have the book". The company said, "We will send you another one by first class special delivery". Yesterday he got both books. The agreement is that he will send one of the books back.

There should have been a deal whereby he sent the book back and paid the postage, or else the company sent the book and paid the postage and the post office received its money.
