Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have this opportunity to speak regarding
the Canadian postal system and to be able to communicate to the Minister a number of concerns that have been brought to my attention over the last number of weeks.
I think it is fair to say as a Member of Parliament that if you were to walk along the main streets of any small village, town, urban area or rural area of Canada and ask people what was on their mind about the federal Government, what kind of a message they would like one to take back to Ottawa, you can be assured that the topic of the post office would come up sometime during that discussion. People will recall that for many years the service provided by the Canadian postal service was nothing less than first class. Canadians were proud of the postal system. As a number of speakers have indicated, Canada was often held up as the model for postal systems which other countries could initiate. They came to Canada looking for guidance.
Unfortunately, that has changed somewhat over the years, unquestionably for the worst. It is interesting to identify some of the reasons why that has taken place. I will come to that eventually.
I want first to look at the mandate of the Corporation and identify two or three areas of that mandate which deserve some comment tonight. One of the areas taken on by the Crown Corporation was to improve postal service in Canada. There are a number of areas where it has done just that. Recently we have seen a new postal code for sending letters to Santa Claus. For the first time one can identify that in our postal history as a major step forward.
Seriously, the delivery time of the postal corporation has increased for first class mail. Over the last number of months it has improved from 80 per cent to 89 per cent in terms of meeting on-time targets. There has been an expansion in some of the urban areas of Canada. Some of the newly emerging landscapes of Canada now receive door-to-door mail service as they find themselves contiguous to existing urban areas. Service is being applied to those areas that certainly ought to qualify.
People still criticize the line-ups in the post office. They are concerned about the level of service. Those people might recall visiting one of the most sacred corporations in this country which is often held up as the best example of corporate efficiency, namely, the Canadian banking system. Notice the long line-ups forming there as you patiently wait to get to a teller or wait at the counter to be served. Before criticizing the services given today by employees in the postal service, let us look at it in comparison with other services being provided.
When looking at the reduced services being experienced in the Canadian postal service over the last number of years, there is one group we ought not to blame. That group is the workers who carry the mail, provide the essential services at the counter and run the thousands of small postal operations across the country.
November 23, 1982

These people are dedicated to their task. I see them time after time throughout all seasons bring the mail to my door in a courteous and serious way. When I visit the small post offices in the rural parts of my constituency, I see dedicated workers. They provide a very positive and useful service to those small communities and rural areas.
Look at the services provided by the people who deliver along the routes in rural Canada. They do more than simply deliver the mail. Their contribution is quite outstanding, particularly in the season we are now approaching.
When we talk about the reduced or decreased services of our postal system, it is important to identify the true cause of that reduction in service. Like any other organization, it has to come from the top. The reason for the difficulties today is that the management of the postal system leaves a great deal to be desired, including both the Conservatives and Liberals which provided the general mandate and down through the senior levels of the post office. Therein lies the critical problems which face us. 1 will have more to say on that in a moment.
1 now want to deal with the human relations that make up another mandate in the postal Corporation. When you look at the record, you find that time lost due to industrial disputes has decreased over the last number of weeks and months. The reason for that is that the whole process of free collective bargaining has been removed from the postal system. As a result of the imposition of the six and five program by the Liberals and Conservatives, free collective bargaining, which is certainly the very basis of labour-management relations in a free country, has been removed from those who work in the postal system. On looking at the whole realm of improved human relations in the postal system, one realizes that a great deal of improvement is possible there. Hopefully, we will see improvements in this area over the next couple of months.
I want to concentrate tonight on the self-sufficiency aspect of the mandate. This is the component which the Liberals and Conservatives feel very strongly about, that the postal system in Canada should break even. In fact, some speakers from the Progressive Conservative Party have indicated that it should make a profit. I wonder whether those same persons feel that the armed services, universities, elementary schools and hospitals in Canada should also make a profit.
There is a certain amount of hypocrisy when individuals in this House demonstrate that they are able to talk out of both sides of their mouth at exactly the same time, on one hand saying that the postal system should make a profit or break even and on the other hand that it should improve the level of service. This blind acceptance by the Government and the Progressive Conservatives that the deficit must be reduced at all costs has resulted in some of the following problems in the postal system of Canada.
Let us look at the increased rates that we have experienced. In 1968 the cost of a first class postage stamp went up to 6 cents, in 1971 to 7 cents, in 1972 to 8 cents, in 1976 to 10 cents, in 1977 to 12 cents, in 1978 to 14 cents, in 1979 to 17 cents, in 1982 to 30 cents, and soon it will go up to 32 cents.

If we look at the increases we find that since the postal service was turned into a Crown corporation, the number of letters mailed increased by 88.2 per cent. If we look at the period since the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) came to power in 1968, we see an increase of 540 per cent. During a time of restraint, an increase of 88 per cent in a two-year period is something we should question, especially when we consider the impact this has on certain groups in society. I refer in particular to our senior citizens. Most of the mail I receive about the cost of postage originates with this group. These people look forward to writing letters and sending parcels to their family and kin across this vast country. They count on the mail. At 32 cents a letter, that will create a very serious hardship for many senior citizens in this country, particularly when we consider that most senior citizens live below the poverty level.
We will also want to recognize that in the attempt to reduce the deficit of the postal service, certain merchants have been subsidized. Bulk mail, which has often been referred to as "junk mail", is subsidized by those people paying 32 cents a letter. In other words, we are saying to the senior citizens of our country, or to the rank and file citizenship across Canada, that we want to increase the cost of their letters in order to enable bulk mail to be delivered at lower rates. Somehow that situation has to be recognized and certainly criticized, that once again the taxpayers of Canada, the rank and file citizens of Canada, are being asked to subsidize the corporate operations of the country.
We have heard a great deal about Saturday closing of wickets in the rural areas of Canada. I suspect that for most Canadians who live in urban centres that does not cause much concern. There is little sensitivity, I suspect, among the people making those decisions, of what it is like to live in small communities or in the rural parts of this country. In my own constituency of Kamloops-Shuswap, for the cattlemen, farmers, miners, loggers or tradesmen who are forced to work out of town, Saturday is often really the only day when they are able to get to the wicket to do their postal business. Saturday, closure, Mr. Speaker, is problematical for these people, indeed.
Also we see the closure of the small rural post office when the single operator is ill. Again, this is a reduction in service. We see the discontinuance of Saturday delivery in the rural areas of Canada. We see that if a carrier is ill no service is going to be provided for that area, and if that carrier who is ill has a business route, someone from a residential route will be taken off, and not replaced, in order to enable that business mail to be delivered. Again this is an obvious reduction in service for Canadians.
We also note that consideration is now being given to alternating daily delivery service. That service will not continue on a Monday through Friday basis in Canada but will likely find itself moving to mail delivery on alternate days only. We hear a great deal about the threat of cutting 1,500 jobs from the postal system. We hear that consideration is being given now to eliminating carrier service to new communities, asking

people to rely on the boxes at the end of the street. We notice that since the six and five program has come in, the rates for mail boxes have gone up substantially more than 6 per cent and 5 per cent, Mr. Speaker. This betrays the true commitment to the six and five program by the Government, resulting in increased costs, and in many cases reduced service to Canadians as a result of its commitment to reduce this deficit.
1 think if the situation is described accurately, Mr. Speaker, we will find that the postal system is being curtailed in an effort to reduce the deficit to zero by 1985. When we consider the difference in service that rural Canadians face in terms of their cable television, power lines, availability of fuels, telephone service, radio service, or most recently the cutbacks in VIA Rail service, we realize that we must guard against any further cutbacks, particularly now as the Government attempts to rationalize the postal Corporation.
Back in October, 1980 we listened very carefully when the Minister responsible for postal services in Canada promised Canadians from the floor of the House of Commons that the Government would ensure that existing levels of service would be maintained. What I would ask the Minister responsible to consider this evening is whether we should not attempt to phase this deficit reduction attempt over a longer period of time. Our rush to make the Crown Corporation a break-even operation, or preferably, as someone said, a make-money operation, results in reduction in services, which is something that Canadians ought not to accept. In a country as vast as Canada where the effort to overcome distance and to increase communication between people ought to be receiving much greater attention from Members of this House, exactly the opposite is taking place. We are making it more difficult for Canadians to communicate and to overcome the distances of our vast country.

Mr. Speaker, just for a few brief moments tonight I would like to make some comments on the Canada Post Corporation which came into effect October 16, 1982, following debate and agreement in the House of Commons, supported by all three parties of the House. I believe that, by and large, we have a very dedicated group of people in Canada Post. I am speaking of the people in the local post offices and the rural mail carriers, and those carriers who do the letter walks in the community in all kinds of weather. 1 believe there has been a tremendous improvement in some sectors over the years, but as Canada grew, there were changes which developed, and the system was not able to keep pace with changes, not only in our society and in our business within Canada, but changes in automation, in methods of handling mail, in transportation within Canada.
I believe there are areas where we can cut the costs and improve the service. If we reflect back a few years, perhaps
some of the deterioration of the present service came at the same time that the mail cars in which we used to sort the mail between cities and towns, were removed from the trains. I believe this is why some of the problems started. If we look at the volume of mail delivered each day between Toronto and Montreal; for example, this mail is loaded on vans, taken to the railway station, loaded on the trains, up to six carloads at a time. You can imagine the number of letters that are there to sort. You have six carloads of mail arriving at the destination at once in these huge postal terminals.
In spite of the automation we have in place, I believe perhaps the time has come to look back to that old system where the mail was loaded in mail cars and the employees sorted the mail between cities so that it arrived at its destination ready to go out to the district offices. Those employees knew when they left that a certain volume of work had to be completed. It was a good system. There were many instances of letters mailed in Toronto in the evening and delivered in Montreal the next morning. As it is now, particularly for some of the smaller communities, the post office trailers are held up longer than they should be, waiting for their load to arrive, waiting to be filled, and consequently we are faced with delay.
At the time the railway service was discontinued we built the huge postal terminals, and perhaps this is when the service started to deteriorate. Not because of the workers or automation but because of the sheer volume which had to be handled out of those areas of concentration. Now in areas such as the Quebec-Windsor Corridor, where we have a large number of passenger trains such as the LRCs, the working conditions on those trains are much better than in years past.
Another area I want to touch on very briefly, Mr. Speaker, is that of small towns and villages, and our rural mail delivery.
I believe the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) touched on that matter briefly when he pointed out how important the mail service was to farmers and small-businessmen who come into the small communities on Saturdays to do their business. Although we are trying to cut costs and we have reverted to the five-day per week delivery in many areas of Canada, I would like to suggest that perhaps we should look at this again. We have very little business conducted in the business community on either Saturday or Sunday. As a result, the mail load on Monday is very light. Therefore, I would suggest we examine the feasibility of reinstating Saturday mail delivery in the rural areas and discontinuing the Monday delivery. Not only is there a lighter load of mail on Mondays as it is on the week's news which is carried in the Saturday papers. Most rural mail carriers deliver Saturday's paper which provides the weekend reading for families, and it is sorely missed in communities across Canada.
I believe if we were to re-examine this situation from the standpoint of discontinuing delivery on Monday rather than on Saturday, it would be a very positive step. The cost-cutting concept is accepted, but it is unfortunate that we did not do

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to join in this debate tonight on the important matter of good postal service. I am pleased the Minister has seen fit to withdraw the definition of a letter, even if that may only be temporary. 1 hope it will not. 1 do not want to re-state many of the well presented arguments by my colleagues and others on such things as cutbacks in service or the many examples of poor postal service, but I would like to refer to the Minister's mid-1982 letter in which he declared that the new regulations provide clarification of our social responsibility to ensure that all Canadians have access to a basic level of postal service at a standard cost. 1 want to deal with these two points, particularly the basic level.
Historically, Mr. Speaker, the basic level of postal service has included the ability of one person to transmit a simple message to another elsewhere in Canada, or in the world for that matter, in time frames consistent with the technology of the day. As technology advanced, packet ships were replaced by coal steamers and stage coaches were replaced by trains. Later those trains and ships were replaced by planes for long distance transportation, and trucks for short-haul. Delivery time frames shrank but costs remained low as volume increased. But always the transmitted article was the same, a simple message, personal, and secure, if desired, in an envelope. Although the speed of mail increased, it was for average or regular mail, and few reasonable people would disagree with that. However, for items requiring extraordinary consideration because of speed or shape, fragility or bulk, or for any other reason, other methods had to be devised. Wherever such special considerations entered into the mail service, trouble followed. It was because of special considerations that special delivery was devised where people could pay extra for extra service.
Couriers, of course, came into being to provide faster, specialized delivery for parcels and letters. It was because of the special considerations of bulk, size, weight or speed that the instrusion of these considerations became a cause of postal decline. Although postal codes and highspeed letter processing machines were designed and installed, volume and special requirements continued to break down the system. The efforts
Supply
of the post office to handle and improve the system were laudable. No doubt Canada Post will continue to work on solutions to provide a basic level of postal service at standard cost.
While it worked on special techniques in the past, this at no time precluded the provision of such special services by private, competing companies which could do the job better. These companies bought high-speed planes, special delivery vehicles, special wire services and now, even satellite and optical message transmission services.
Not many years ago when the post office was approached by Canadian banks to develop a high-speed means of handling interbank transactions so that bank customers could be given much better banking services, consistent with the modern age, the post office declined to provide such service and the banks had to proceed on their own.
Now that EFT, electronic funds transfer, and other highspeed banking services have become established techniques, the Government wishes to pirate this private and efficient system. It wants to attempt to superimpose it or fit it into the basic level of postal service, with the obvious consequence of reducing efficiency and further complicating an already overloaded and inefficient system where specialty services are concerned. A bank transaction is not a letter, be it 500 grams or not. A bank withdrawal made in Calgary from an account in Vancouver is not a letter, even if a paper printout is made. Similarly, a recapitulation of all the day's transactions, when processed electronically, is not a letter or a number of letters.
Would Canada Post plan to charge 30 cents per line for the number of transactions in a day? If so, we can think of what such costs would add to bank charges.
If the monopoly enjoyed by Canada Post is to be used to pirate this service, reduce its efficiency and raise its cost, then clearly such monopoly must be opposed. The continuing preoccupation of the Government with state, bureaucratic, noncompetitive services will surely retard the development of modern communication services compared to those of other countries.
The dictionary defines a letter as a "written or printed message addressed to a person or persons, usually sent by post or messenger and fairly long". But then, any reasonable person knows what a letter is. What is the new definition of a letter which the Minister is promoting? It states that it is "mailable matter in any form, the mass of which, if any ... ". Clearly, a letter is no longer a letter. The world can call a letter a letter, but Canada Post and the Government know better. They can ignore reality and extend bureaucratic monopoly to the homes and offices of the nation.
What is this "massless" communication, and when will it come into being? It is here now, Mr. Speaker, It is not a thing of the future. It is simply the sending of a message from one point to another without it ever having been transcribed on solid material. In other words, it was entirely energy from start to finish-not mass or substance.

An example of such communication would be sending a message by computer, through electrical or optical means, to a receiving computer which would not print it out on paper but would, rather, display it on a CRT, a television screen.
What jurisdiction or control should Canada Post, which the Minister says is mandated to provide a basic level of postal service, have over such privately sent, privately funded, privately designed and never "posted" communications?
The exclusive privilege granted Canada Post was intended to allow it to provide basic services for simple "letters" so that private business would not skim off the lucrative trade between such cities as Toronto and Montreal while leaving costly, small rural communities unserviced.
The definition of a letter-which has been withdrawn- described it as "mailable matter in any form, the mass of which, if any . . . whether or not enclosed in an envelope. .." leaves the power-hungry Government and bureaucratically obsessed Minister with all the latitude necessary to eliminate private, confidential, speedy, modern, world-class communication in Canada.
Also, when the absolute monopoly has been established and all the competition eliminated, we will have "Communi-Can", the PetroCan of communications, where the taxpayer will pay far too much for letters, just as he now pays far too much for gasoline.
I hope that the Minister has now really taken to heart the seriousness of the myriad representations made by responsible, non-partisan, greatly involved organizations and companies such as the Retail Council of Canada, General Motors of Canada, Canadian Tire Corporation and over 300 others, which have different motives from the Government. Their motive is to reduce the cost to taxpayers, not to increase it. They have clearly outlined the unacceptability of a definition which includes "massless" excludes the privacy of envelopes, and indicates no limit to the horrendous cost of Government intervention and possible censorship.
At a time when Canada is actively promoting Telidon, the world's best videotech system which will, one day, include electronic mail to every home that has an outlet, we have one bureaucratic, antediluvian Minister erecting roadblocks in the way of another who is trying to "sell the future" and develop Canada's skills in high technology.
If we had a Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who understood the complexities and opportunities offered by advanced thinking instead of revelling in stultified, restrictionist ideology, such retrograde legislation would never have been introduced in the first place.
Canada has been suffocated in research and advance-job creation by the neglect of creative thinkers and the elevation of its socialist dinosaurs to positions of power.
While I would encourage Canada Post to get on with its attempts to generate efficiency in the basic postal system for handling regular, everyday dictionary definition letters, I totally oppose its dabbling in areas which are far beyond its
competence, particularly when it has not yet solved the basic problems that lie within its simple mandate.
The plundering of productive businesses, large and small, to subsidize inefficiency; the use of deficit taxpayers' dollars to expand into unneeded areas of electronic communications which are already well handled; those specialized courier services, and the restriction on the freedom of a person or tradesperson to drop a note at the door of a friend or to leave an invoice at a customer's door, on penalty of a fine, are the reasons that Canada is falling back in its standard of living while other nations move ahead. That is why the people of Canada have lost faith in the backward-facing policies of this head-in-the-sand Government.
This is why I intend to support this motion of censure against the Government which has raised postal rates 500 per cent in the Prime Minister's term of office. Now that he has wrestled inflation and employment to the ground perhaps he can start on postal rates.
Canada's postal service and its employees operate at a high level of efficiency. They would do even better if a letter were defined as being perhaps 50 grams' weight enclosed in a standardized envelope.
I look forward to the day when regular mail at low cost will provide the nonspecialized service that is needed right across the country. 1 urge the Government to let Canada Post get on with its principal task of serving the nation with a basic level of postal service at a standard low cost.

subtopic: PUBLIC ACCOUNTS-AUDITOR GENERAL'S CERTIFICATE. (B) GOVERNMENT RESPONSE
PUBLIC ACCOUNTS-AUDITOR GENERAL'S CERTIFICATE. (B) GOVERNMENT RESPONSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some weeks ago when the Public Accounts for Canada ending March 31, 1982 were tabled, I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) about the accounting practices of the Government and its agencies.
In his certificate, the Auditor General said that he believed the "stated accounting policies are not appropriate for a fair presentation of the assets and liabilities and revenues and expenditures of the Government of Canada." He went on to
November 23, 1982

say that they were inadequate in two very specific areas. First, significant departmental activities were reported in separate financial statements or accounts that are not combined in the Government's financial statements. Separate financial statements or accounts are presented in other sections of the Public Accounts in such areas as the Exchange Fund Account, the Canada Pension Plan Account, the Unemployment Insurance Account, the Canadian Ownership Account and other similar Accounts.
Second, the Auditor General stated that investments to Crown-owned corporations and agencies as of March 31, 1982 amounted to approximately $25 billion or 63 per cent of the Government's net recorded assets. The assets, liabilities, revenues and expenditures of these entities are not consolidated in the accompanying financial statements.
This points to very real abuses or misconceptions which the Government puts forth in presenting its financial statements. I would not dare to say that the Government is trying to hide anything because in some areas it understates its assets and in other areas it actually overstates them. An example of the Government overstating its accounts could be found where there are excess amounts advanced over asset value received that confers a benefit and constitutes expenditure in respect of international development assistance, which should be recorded and reported as such on the Statement of Revenue and Expenditure.
The Auditor General also estimated that if international development assistance loans and subscriptions were reported in this manner, reported assets would decrease and accumulated deficit would increase by approximately $3.9 billion as at March 31, 1982.
A second example of where the Government is in error in overstating its assets is that financial obligations are not recorded in respect of amounts payable under statutory appropriations, earned and unpaid annual vacation leave, employee termination benefits and actuarial liabilities arising from the indexing provisions of employee pension plans. Also in the view of the Auditor General, all these financial obligations should be appropriately recorded and reported in the financial statements to provide a more complete disclosure of Government liabilities. Ele estimated that if these obligations were recorded, the reported liabilities and accumulated deficit would be increased by at least another $14.5 billion as at March 31, 1982.
An example of the Government being in error in underestimating its assets is in the area of revenue for the year from oil export charges, a federal Government tax. It excluded receipts of some $445 million which are included in the "specified purpose" liability account. Its failure to include this amount in revenue is inadequate in the opinion of the Auditor General and not in accordance with accounting policies. There should be another $445 million in revenue.
This leaves the books of the Government of Canada in a position where its actual assets are overstated by some $17.6
Adjournment Debate
billion. 1 think the Government should address itself to improving the bookkeeping practices, administrative policies and accounting principles it uses.
Right now, I think most people are aware that the private sector uses generally accepted accounting principles. Within the Government of Canada there are no generally accepted accounting principles. I would urge the Government to address this problem and rectify it so that all accounts of the Government of Canada, anywhere Canadian taxes are spent, have a standard form by which the Government accounts for that.
The second proposal which would significantly help reporting the Government's accounts fairly would be to incorporate Crown corporation legislation.
In conclusion, as it stands now, if any company or any individual submitted a tax return to the Department of National Revenue based on financial statements similar to the way the Government of Canada draws them up, they would certainly be prosecuted for income tax evasion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rendering his opinion of the Government's 1981-82 financial statement, the Auditor General expressed four basic concerns. First, the Auditor General concluded that loans to developing countries, because of their concessionary terms, should be reported on the books of Canada at a value that discounts for the benefits conferred on the recipient. This is in fact inflation accounting which yet has to receive broad application in either the private or public sector.
It is generally acknowledged, however, that while inflation accounting would tend to reduce the value of financial assets such as developing loans, it would have an offsetting impact on financial liabilities such as outstanding debt.
The Auditor General expressed the view that financial obligations arising from statutory appropriations not now reported have the effect of understating liabilities. The exclusion of certain liabilities as well as assets resulting from the current stated accounting policies, accounting policies designed to comply with enabling legislation, is fully recognized in the notes accompanying the financial statements. The current method of accounting for the Supplementary Retirement Benefit Accounts, with which the Attorney General takes exception, results from a simple compliance with enabling legislation, legislation passed by this House.
Third, the Attorney General feels that consideration should be given to extending the definition of the Government as an accounting entity. The Comptroller General has made an undertaking before the Standing Committee on Public Accounts to once again review the appropriateness of the financial statements in satisfying the needs of the users.

subtopic: CANADIAN TRANSPORT COMMISSION-SEVERITY OF PENALTY IMPOSED ON AIR B.C. (B) COMMISSION'S POWERS
CANADIAN TRANSPORT COMMISSION-SEVERITY OF PENALTY IMPOSED ON AIR B.C. (B) COMMISSION'S POWERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday last 1 had occasion to draw the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) to a letter he had received from the Greater Victoria Chamber of Commerce relating to a penalty which had been imposed upon Air B.C. for having offered on the first of April, 1982, a special fare to travel between Victoria and Vancouver. This special fare, by way of a prank, if you like, or a promotional operation, was considered for a number of months by the Canadian Transport Commission before it decided what it should do. 1 will leave to one side for a moment what the Minister said with regard to the stupidity of the question, because that is quite another matter.
In order to deal with this question properly I think we have to bear in mind some rules which govern the decisions of the Canadian Transport Commission. The Minister reminded me of one of them. He said that one of the rules is against predatory prices. This was not a predatory price for all time. This was a price for one occasion. However, the fundamental rule to which the Canadian Transport Commission is committed is that any regulation should be determined on the basis of "public convenience" and necessity.
I speak, with the prompting of the Victoria Chamber of Commerce, on behalf of the travelling public. An editorial this morning in the Colonist Times was brought to me by a friend who travels from Victoria. It states that the Canadian Transport Commission is "grounding people" because the penalty, which was eventually levied against Air B.C., was that on December 21 that flight of Air B.C. should be grounded. That is draconian. This decision, however, was not rendered until October 18. It took from April 1 until October to end the shillying and shallying this way and that and to decide what would be done. Then, on October 18, a penalty was levied that there would be no Rights on that particular route on December 21.
I suppose one could say that the airline did breach some regulation for one day in a lighthearted way. However, to inRict a penalty of that sort, to that extent, at that season, is quite unacceptable. The travelling public will be grounded on that particular date. Air B.C. came in to fill some gaps between Air Canada and CP Air connecting the mainland and the island. Air B.C. fills those gaps, and to eliminate that particular service so close to Christmas time when families are
coming together is a shocking approach to this particular matter, to my way of thinking.
I want to stress that I am not speaking on behalf of Air B.C. It was the Greater Victoria Chamber of Commerce which had written a letter to the Minister and I received a copy of it. For very obvious reasons Air B.C. must keep its head down; it must deal with the Canadian Transport Commission. I understand it has made some suggestion regarding some other days when it might be prepared to be shutdown. However, it seems to be quite beyond the merits of the case to have it shut down right in the middle of the Christmas season. There must be some other way of dealing with it. It might be appropriate for the penalty to be imposed some other time in January, after the Christmas season, for example. 1 remind Hon. Members that the governing and guiding principle of the Canadian Transport Commission is "public convenience and necessity". I ask, how the public convenience and public necessity are to be served by prohibiting these Rights on December 21 ?
I received a letter from the Minister which he must have written Friday afternoon because I received it on Monday morning. I am not disclosing anything which has not already been disclosed by the press because he did make his letter public, but he admitted with regret, and I give him honour for it, that the answer he gave me was "somewhat misleading". He said in the House he had asked the CTC to review this particular decision. In fact, he admitted in the letter, as reported in that paragraph, "I have not asked for a review because 1 am not empowered to do so on my own intiative". He could have asked, through Cabinet, that there be a Cabinet decision to rescind or alter that particular decision, but he stepped back from that because, as he said, it was to be word only in situations of national importance. It may not be nationally important in the eyes of the Minister, the matter of communications between Vancouver Island and the Mainland. It is of great importance, however, and I hope the Minister learns this one day, to those who live on the mainland or on the island, particularly at Christmastime, that those facilities of air transport be available.
I do hope that one way or another, possibly with just a little nudge by the Minister, the CTC can be a little more reasonable, a little more charitable; remembering that the Christmas spirit is there, and that it should not act like Scrooge, as it is about to by insisting on that particular penalty. Perhaps, it could be just a little more charitable at that season of the year.
I hope it will allow Air B.C. to Ry on December 21 and to take its penalty, whatever it may be, at another season.

THE ECONOMY-GOVERNMENT POLICY SPENDING AFFECTING PRIVATE SECTOR. (B) INTEREST RATE LEVELS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 27 I had occasion to ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) questions with respect to the principles on which the financial affairs of the country are being managed. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, in the Minister's address to this House the Minister stated that as one of the basic principles of economic management we must continue to rely primarily on the dynamism and the creativity of the private sector as engines of growth in Canada. He went on to say that the Government will be seeking areas where it can act in close co-operation with business and labour to improve the financial help of the private sector as well as its ability to expand and prosper.
1 asked the Minister really what had he done for the private sector. I pointed out to the Minister that the effect of his Budget was to put $400 million into Canadair and de Havi-land, both losers as far as profitability is concerned, and both Crown corporations. I pointed out to the Minister that within a day or so after the Budget we learned that Petro Canada had purchased certain gas stations owned by British Petroleum at a cost in excess of $600 million. I pointed out that in the budget the Minister increased unemployment insurance premiums by $1.7 billion. That is a further tax on employment. It increases the wage wedge to $5.52 per $100 for wages paid.
The Minister replied that he was a good fellow, that he had spent $1.2 billion in make-work programs to increase employment. The fact is the budget only talked about $500 million. I
Adjournment Debate
do not know where the other money came from. Perhaps the Minister was looking at his budgetary figures. His budget increased the amount to offset unemployment by $500 million. He went on to say something about $400 million going to the railways and that this was important. One of the major railways is a Crown corporation. The other is a corporation run by Mr. Sinclair, a friend of the Government.
Perhaps it will accomplish something, but I do not see anywhere in the budget the dynamism and creativity of the private sector being encouraged or the financial health of the private sector being able to expand and prosper. The Minister knows that. The Government only pays lip service to private enterprise, lip service to dynamism in the private sector. In fact, it really does not care about the private sector, particularly in terms of employment.
A tax on employing people was levied in this budget to the extent of $1.7 billion. That tax will increase unemployment in this country by approximately 46,700 people during the next year. The Minister may ask how I figure that out. The answer is simple; the same way the Minister figured out that by spending $500 million he would create 60,000 jobs for a total of 18 months or between 17,000 and 18,000 person-years of work.
As a rule of thumb, a 1 per cent increase in real gross national product yields a 1 per cent increase in employment. If you take the 1971 base calculations as determined by the Conference Board and relate the present GNP to 1971, this year we would have about $130.4 billion in GNP. The effect of the $1.7 billion charge has to be a detriment to the GNP of .0447. If you do the mathematics, you will find if you multiply by the current number of people unemployed that you will have lost 46,700 person-years of work.
The effect of the budget presented by the Government will be that it costs jobs in Canada, costs the private sector, hurts the Canadian economy and is a total detriment. It will boost the public sector, boost Crown corporations, create more Government in our lives and work in exact opposition to the principles the Minister enunciated, principles that we could go along with, but principles he clearly does not believe in.
